I'm happy to say for 2025 that we have maintained our broad access for Wegovy, covering 55 million people with obesity. There were no major changes with opt-ins and opt-outs. It's important to note that these patients have Wegovy available at a low out-of-pocket cost. More than 80% of them paying less than $25 for a prescription. This is also, in addition, we have now more than 20 states that also cover Wegovy through Medicaid. You also had a question about compounding.
Our latest market intelligence does tell us and show us that it is having impact and it is growing faster than we had anticipated. I want to remind everyone that we do not supply compounding, and we have significant actions in place to curtail this. Our focus is on patient safety and educating patients and providers that this is not semaglutide, and also to work with the regulators to curtail compounding as well.
Jacob Martin Wiborg Rode
VP of Investor Relations, Novo Nordisk
Thank you, Dave, and thank you, Richard, for those two questions. We turn to the next questions, please.
Operator
Thank you. Your next question comes from Emily Field from Barclays. Please go ahead.
Emily Field
Director, Head of U.S. Biopharmaceuticals Equity Research, Barclays
Thank you for my questions. Just to follow up on the compounding point, for a few months now, all the doses of semaglutide have been, marked as available on the FDA drug shortage website, but the molecule is still marked as in shortage. When do you expect that to be removed? Would that lead to a similar kind of off-ramp from the FDA for the compounders that we saw FDA issue a directive in December for tirzepatide? Secondly, another question on REDEFINE 1.
the gray curve for the patients that were on a lower dose at the end of treatment, is it fair to say that a significant number of those patients did go up to 2.4 and then titrated down, whether for tolerability or, , they were very, very fast responders to the weight loss? Thank you.
Jacob Martin Wiborg Rode
VP of Investor Relations, Novo Nordisk
Thank you, Emily. On the first one, the follow-up question on compounding, we'll turn to you, Dave.
David Moore
SVP, Commercial, Novo Nordisk
Yeah. As you mentioned, we are still listed on the drug shortage list. We are in active dialogue with FDA. It is ongoing. Of course, as we increase the resilience in our supply, that has an impact on our ability to get off the drug shortage list. We are focused on doing that as fast as possible, as we believe this will help our further actions to curtail compounding in the future.
Jacob Martin Wiborg Rode
VP of Investor Relations, Novo Nordisk
Thank you, Dave. On the early responder curve, we'll turn to you, Martin.
Martin Holst Lange
EVP, Head of Development, Novo Nordisk
Yeah, absolutely. I wanna go back to Lars' point that obesity is a complex disease and patients have individual response to treatment. In the group where patients did not titrate to full dose at end of trial, the mean dose at week 20 was around 1.5 mg, indicating that very few actually opted to try to titrate to the full 2.4 mg dose. This is more to be seen as a group of fast and high responders.
Therefore, with the weight loss that they accrued, which was then also faster than the other group. They started to slow down to balance the speed of their weight loss, their gastrointestinal side effects, but also the fact that they were approaching a level below the definition of obesity. Therefore, again, it speaks to the very powerful biology that we see, but also the need to individualize treatment. And again, I'll just remind you, this is the trial at a population level where we've seen very few gastrointestinal side effects at the level of Wegovy, and therefore that is not the key driver of how patients choose to titrate. Well, I think Lars has a very good point. Patients know how to do this together with their physicians.
Jacob Martin Wiborg Rode
VP of Investor Relations, Novo Nordisk
Thanks a lot, Martin, and thank you, Emily, for the two sets of questions. With that, we are ready for the next questions, please.
Operator
Thank you. Your next question comes from the line of Florent Cespedes from Bernstein. Please go ahead.
Florent Cespedes
Senior Sell-Side Analyst European BioPharmaceuticals, Bernstein
Good afternoon. Thank you for taking my questions. Two quick ones, please. First for Dave. Could you give us your view on the situation in the U.S. for semaglutide regarding IRA, Inflation Reduction Act? Because now you are on the list. So could you remind us how you will manage the situation for 2027, and when should we have the final level of rebates? Could you remind us the process would be great. Second question for Martin, on monlunabant. Maybe could you give us some color on the Phase II E from the kidney trial, notably on the tolerance, if there is any doubt on the tolerance side that could maybe help you to design or adjust the rest of the ongoing clinical trial? Thank you.
Jacob Martin Wiborg Rode
VP of Investor Relations, Novo Nordisk
Thanks a lot, Florent. On the first one, IRA, of course, hard to speculate too much, but with that over to you, Dave.
David Moore
SVP, Commercial, Novo Nordisk
Yeah. Thank you, Florent. As expected, semaglutide containing products, Ozempic, Rybelsus, and Wegovy, they are selected for the second round of CMS negotiations. It's too early to speculate on the potential impact. As we've stated in the past, we oppose government price setting, like we have from the beginning. The process, though, is as follows. The negotiations will end in the beginning of November. The maximum fair price will be published by the end of November, and it will be effective in 1 January 2027. Just for background, the rough U.S. channel mix across our portfolio is about 50% commercial, 30% Medicare, 10% Medicaid, and 10% other.
Jacob Martin Wiborg Rode
VP of Investor Relations, Novo Nordisk
Thank you, Dave.
David Moore
SVP, Commercial, Novo Nordisk
Sure.
Jacob Martin Wiborg Rode
VP of Investor Relations, Novo Nordisk
On the next question on monlunabant in the diabetic kidney disease, we'll turn to you, Martin.
Martin Holst Lange
EVP, Head of Development, Novo Nordisk
Yeah. Thank you very much for that question. Two reminders, one being we never did the acquisition of monlunabant to develop it purely for diabetic kidney disease. Our focus was on the weight loss potential. Second, I'll just remind you that these are small studies. Obviously we are not discouraged by the fact that we did not see impact on the actual diabetic kidney disease. The study did confirm a weight loss potential for monlunabant.
When we look at the safety and tolerability profile, it was comparable, albeit with slightly lower rates than in the dedicated obesity study, basically indicating that we can still have an aspiration of exploring this further in Phase IIB, with lower doses, looking at weight loss potential, but obviously also, and this has been the intent from the get-go, also ruling out a potential safety concern.
Florent Cespedes
Senior Sell-Side Analyst European BioPharmaceuticals, Bernstein
Thank you very much.
Jacob Martin Wiborg Rode
VP of Investor Relations, Novo Nordisk
Thank you, Martin. Yeah, thank you as well, Florent. We're ready for the next set of questions, please.
Operator
Thank you. Your next question comes from the line of Evan Seigerman from BMO Capital Markets. Please go ahead.
Evan Seigerman
Managing Director, Head of Healthcare Research, BMO Capital Markets
Hi, all. Thank you so much for taking my questions. Kind of a big picture question. There seems to be an obsession with absolute weight loss, whether a percent more or less can make a winner or loser. I'm specifically referring to CagriSema. Maybe walk me through how you view the ideal product profile of an asset. Is it better weight loss, no plateauing, tolerability, longer acting, better delivery? As you think about your portfolio, what would you like to see in kind of your next generation product? Thank you.
Jacob Martin Wiborg Rode
VP of Investor Relations, Novo Nordisk
Thank you, Evan. I think on the high level, obesity question, we'll turn to you, Lars. Yeah.
Lars Fruergaard Jørgensen
CEO, Novo Nordisk
Thank you, Evan, for bringing that up. I think it's a really, really good topic to discuss, and obviously it's a quite broad topic. I think the discussion opens up with what we now see in terms of efficacious biologics, because you could say that with former generation products like Wegovy, you could in principle say load patients up and all would say w tolerate the weight loss they see. Also the GI tolerability we know is very good. But when you get into say the next generation products, where you amplify the weight loss, you tease out the difference between different patients who w we are still trying to look into the omics and figure out what defines the difference.
We have a lot of data, so we can start actually finding ideas about who will respond in certain ways and, , from a speed of weight loss, et cetera. That then we're into the topic of, say, quality of weight loss. I think in the early days of obesity, we have all been obsessed by the percentage over time. I think that's a problematic ratio because if you have lived with obesity a good part of your life and suddenly you lose, say, 25%, some even more weight loss in a matter of, say, half a year to a year, that's a very dramatic, say, change in your life and not necessarily what anyone would like. That's one.
Martin Holst Lange
EVP, Head of Development, Novo Nordisk
Then of course, we have all the comorbidities. Increasingly, I think with the establishment of CV benefits, liver benefits, et cetera, it also becomes a matter of, say, the health outcome improvements you have. In this, say, opportunity space, I think it's important to be able to address those opportunities with different type of agents, to cater for these differences. Short term, as I mentioned before, I think, patients together with the physician are quite comfortable in managing this journey. I think we are perhaps struggling a bit in doing the perfect segmentation of what this market will look like. I think we can look into all the data we have and find ways to also more targeted direct, specific products to certain, subsegments.
I think this is another example of the fact that we're in the early days of understanding obesity, how patients are different. I think it's all opportunity for us with the breadth of the portfolio we have and all the data we have. Yes, percentage of weight loss matters, but quality of weight loss and benefit on comorbidities, et cetera, also matters. It's in that total equation that I think we have a really exciting opportunity for continuous leadership in the space. Thank you, Evan.
Jacob Martin Wiborg Rode
VP of Investor Relations, Novo Nordisk
Thank you, Lars, and thank you, Evan, for the questions. We have time for two more sets of questions, and let's start with the first one, please.
Operator
Thank you. The next question comes from the line of Luisa Hector from Berenberg. Please go ahead.
Luisa Hector
Head of Global Pharma Equity Research, Berenberg
Hello. Thanks for taking my questions. For REDEFINE 1, could you just comment on what percentage of patients down titrated and any color on the timing at which that happened, and perhaps on the highest dose, what the discontinuation rate was? I wonder if I could ask you on a question on amycretin and progression there. When I pull together your comments on CagriSema, the high potency individual patient responses, and then we layer in the proposed FDA guidelines that say Phase II data should be sufficient to capture maximal or near maximal weight reduction effects with the dosing regime. Do you feel that you have enough data to progress into Phase III, or would perhaps another Phase II be advisable? Thank you.
Jacob Martin Wiborg Rode
VP of Investor Relations, Novo Nordisk
Thank you for those two questions, Luisa. I think both of them are for you, Martin. Let's start with the first one, on the data in REDEFINE 1.
Sachin Jain
Equity Research Analyst, Bank of America
Yeah. First of all, we had these two very clear distinct groups. The larger group of 57% of the people titrating to 2.4. Just to give you an example, they were at a mean dose of 2.2 mg at 20 weeks. They then continued to the full 2.4 and appeared to stay on that. There were a few patients doing ups and downs, but it would not be meaningful to try to tease them out. Similarly, just wanna remind you at week 20, the other group were at 1.5, and they down titrated a little bit as a group to, at end of trial, 1.1.
Martin Holst Lange
EVP, Head of Development, Novo Nordisk
While basically securing a weight loss that was higher than what we've seen before, namely 25.2%. At the same time, this way of allowing patients to do, I don't wanna say personalized titration, but close to, actually allowed us to see the lowest overall dropout ever seen in a Phase III pivotal trial, but also very low, and again the lowest gastrointestinal dropouts seen in a pivotal trial. Just a reminder, CagriSema in REDEFINE 1, 3.6% dropout, semaglutide in STEP 1, 4.5% dropout due to gastrointestinal side effects. We're actually quite encouraged by the data.
As Lars also alluded to, by employing this individual approach to patients moving forward, we can really leverage the full benefit of not only CagriSema, but also our pipeline products.
Jacob Martin Wiborg Rode
VP of Investor Relations, Novo Nordisk
Thanks for that, Martin. Thanks a lot. On the second question on amycretin, we turn to you, Martin, again, and on the next steps.
Martin Holst Lange
EVP, Head of Development, Novo Nordisk
Yes. As we have generated data on the oral version of amycretin. They're very consistent with the data that we see with the subcutaneous version of amycretin in patients with obesity. We have an ongoing phase II trial in patients with Type 2 diabetes. Our current assessment is that we live up to the spirit of the FDA draft guidance. Obviously, as in any progression of clinical development, we have to discuss with the regulatory authorities, which we do in short order.
Jacob Martin Wiborg Rode
VP of Investor Relations, Novo Nordisk
Thank you, Martin, and thanks to you as well, Luisa. We are ready for a final set of questions, please.
Operator
Thank you. Your final questions today come from the line of Michael Novod from Nordea. Please go ahead.
Michael Novod
SVP and Head of Investor Relations, Nordea.
Thank you very much. Michael Novod from Nordea. Also two questions. The first one with the data on hand with CagriSema and the flexibility and more sort of individualized treatment as well as sort of your plans for amycretin, have you changed any sort of view on whether to how to sort of whether the LOE on semaglutide in 2032 and the way of sort of replacing Wegovy with either of these drugs? And then secondly, can you tease out also on when you look at the very early data on CagriSema and also amycretin, anything more to add on whether amycretin looks different in terms of tolerability?
I know it's very early data you have, but more to sort of try to pin down on how this could look in later stage trials, whether it's just as tolerable as CagriSema.
Jacob Martin Wiborg Rode
VP of Investor Relations, Novo Nordisk
Hi, Michael. Thanks for those two questions. I think first, on the overall view on CagriSema and amycretin, we'll turn to you, Camilla, and afterwards on amycretin tolerability, we'll turn to you, Martin. Over to you, Camilla.
Camilla Sylvest
EVP, and Head of Commercial Strategy and Corporate Affairs, Novo Nordisk
Yeah, thanks a lot. In terms of whether we have changed anything in our view towards loss of exclusivity, I would say we have not. What we have learned now is, of course, that, little bit more clarity on different segments. We talked about individualized treatment. We learned more about how each product works. But it only gives rise to us, getting more information about how we are going to position this broad portfolio of opportunities that we have. The short answer is no, and we also continue to, of course, build on, semaglutide franchise. You just saw the new indications that we got. Full speed on that going forward, but also full speed on the new innovations, simply establishing this full portfolio. No radical changes to that at all.
Jacob Martin Wiborg Rode
VP of Investor Relations, Novo Nordisk
Thank you, Camilla. On the amycretin data to you, Martin.
Martin Holst Lange
EVP, Head of Development, Novo Nordisk
Yeah, it's early days. Obviously what we can say at this point in time is we're working with two powerful biologics. They appear to have similar efficacy, but also safety and tolerability potential. Obviously that also means that we have to think in the power of the combination biology into our amycretin development program to accrue the full potential, both in terms of weight loss, but also safety and tolerability, and potentially also comorbidities when we do develop amycretin and CagriSema moving forward.
Jacob Martin Wiborg Rode
VP of Investor Relations, Novo Nordisk
Thank you, Martin, and also thank you to you, Michael. Now that concludes the Q&A session. Thank you for participating and feel free to contact investor relations regarding any follow-up questions that you may have. Before we fully close the call, I would like to hand over the word to you, Lars, for final remarks.
Lars Fruergaard Jørgensen
CEO, Novo Nordisk
Yeah. Thank you, Jacob. I'm very pleased with 2024 sales growth of 26% driven by our GLP-1 portfolio in both operating units. Within R&D we see a strong momentum as we just discussed in our pipeline, as underlined by the recent readouts in obesity, both for CagriSema and amycretin. Of course I'm also very pleased with the expected 2025 outlook. We continue to focus heavily on commercial execution and on the progression of our R&D pipeline and the expansion of our production capacity. The plan is very clear, and we know what it takes to execute on this. Also thank you from me on behalf of management for your time today. We appreciate the opportunity to discuss our business with you. Thank you very much. Bye-bye.
Operator
Thank you. This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for participating. You may now disconnect.

content.text:
James Quigley
Executive Director of European Pharma and Biotech Equity Research, Goldman Sachs
Good morning, everybody. I'm James Quigley, European Pharma Analyst here at Goldman Sachs, and it's a pleasure to welcome you all here to the Novo Q2 management meeting. Today we're joined by Lars Jørgensen, CEO, Karsten Knudsen, CFO, Camilla Sylvest, Head of Commercial, and also Martin Lange, Head of Development. With that all explained, I'll hand straight over to you guys to kick off.
Lars Jørgensen
President and CEO, Novo
Good.
James Quigley
Executive Director of European Pharma and Biotech Equity Research, Goldman Sachs
Thank you.
Lars Jørgensen
President and CEO, Novo
Thank you, James, and thank you, Goldman Sachs for hosting us today. We're excited to be here. You have probably seen some of our slides. We'll go through them quickly just to set the stage and then get to the Q&A. The first slide is the forward-looking statements. You know, we'll be talking about the future. Could turn out to be different than what we preach here, so be aware of that, and there are more notes in our website, et cetera. You know our strategic aspirations. We feel we're making good progress serving more patients, strong commercial execution. We're really glad about how we're strengthening our market position in diabetes, how we're growing in obesity.
We have a few challenges in rare diseases, but we are encouraged by future growth, not least because of the great data we have received on Mim8 over the past quarter. Excited about that. You can say all of the financial execution turns into that we have upgraded our outlook for the year. You should see that as sign of confidence in the momentum we have in the business and also having supply of products to fuel that continued growth. With that, I'll leave the word to Camilla for some comments on the commercial area.
Camilla Sylvest
EVP and Head of Commercial Strategy and Corporate Affairs, Novo
Yeah. Thank you, Lars. Here you see our sales growth of 25%, how it's distributed on regions and therapy areas. 36% growth in North America, 11% growth in international operations. Growth driven by all regions. When it comes to therapy areas, really our key brands, so Ozempic, Rybelsus, Wegovy, that is driving our growth. You see a strong growth in GLP-1 diabetes, where we also continue to exceed our leadership in diabetes care now with a market share in total diabetes above 34%. If we zoom in on obesity, we have, you know, 37% growth.
If we take a look at the US on the next slide, you can see that we are continuing to expand the number of of starter doses into the market and also on total scripts we now have since the beginning of the year, a doubling of the total scripts. We are progressing very nicely in terms of our ability to provide Wegovy to patients in the US, but also in the rest of the world, where we now have launched in 14 countries and are continuing to launch in more and more countries as we speak. With that, over to Dr. Lange to give us an update on R&D.
Martin Lange
EVP and Head of Development, Novo
Thank you very much, Camilla. If I could have the next slide. As Lars already alluded to, we're very happy with the results that we saw from phase II, our Mim8 pivotal trial. It was a complex trial investigating the broad range of hemophilia with and without inhibitors across the spectrum of hemophilia in terms of severity. We had both males and females in the study, and we were investigating patients coming from either prophylaxis or on-demand treatment. We're also investigating both once weekly and once monthly.
Quite complex study with a lot of permutations when it comes to the primary endpoint. At the end of the day, what you should take away is for the primary endpoint, regardless of looking at once weekly or once monthly, comparing to prophylaxis treatment or previous on-demand treatment, we see the mean annual bleed rate reduction of somewhere between 60% and 90+% , which is obviously exceedingly gratifying even for patients coming from previous on-demand treatment. Sorry, prophylaxis treatment.
If we look at the median annual bleed rate, it was zero across the board, indicating that, regardless of which analysis we did, more than 50% of patients had zero bleeds. If we look at the actual numbers, again, it's between 60+% and 90+% of patients that have zero bleeds. Very, very strong efficacy data. Similarly, we saw a strong safety profile with no thromboembolic events. Somewhere between 5% and 12%, again, depending on the analysis, percent of patients reporting injection site reactions. A very attractive number. Really, really happy with these data and obviously moving towards a submission during the H1 of 2025. If I could have the next slide. We see broad pipeline progress.
Of course, really happy with the almost global approval for insulin icodec. I have to mention a complete response letter in the US focusing on manufacturing and also obviously type 1 diabetes. We expect to be able to resubmit the icodec file in the US during the course of H1 of 2025. Broadly speaking, we see a lot of progress in our pipeline. I wanna call out obviously the data that we'll see from monlunabant in this half of the year, first on obesity and secondly on diabetic kidney disease, two phase II studies that will read out in Q3 and Q4 respectively. Looking very much forward to see our first CagriSema data, the REDEFINE 1 trial that will read out in December of this year.
I've already talked to Mim8, but maybe also mentioning that we have resubmitted concizumab in the US for both hemophilia with inhibitors, but also without inhibitors. Finally, we've initiated the Artemis study, which is a study in acute myocardial infarction with ziltivekimab. I think with that, over to you, Karsten.
Karsten Knudsen
EVP and CFO, Novo
Yeah. Thank you, Martin. When we look at the results in the first six months, then we delivered fantastic 25% sales growth. This is really industry-leading sales growth and a continuation of the sales growth we saw in Q1. The 25% has a benefit from rebate adjustments related to the US and also benefits from a reasonably easy comparator from last year linked to phasing of rebates last year. I'll come back to why that's important. Our commercial investments are at a low level in that respect, 6%, adjusted for certain legal provisions last year, around 10%.
Really indicating we have the commercial infrastructure in place, perhaps with, unless we talk about obesity, where we're really investing in obesity market development activities, across the board. R&D really stepping up 78% is overstating the true R&D step up P&L-wise due to the fact that we had an impairment on ocedurenone and also another asset in Q2. Adjusting for that, the R&D is still stepping up more than 30%, which is linked to our intent to really build a competitive pipeline for the company's future growth for the coming decades. Net-net, that yields operating profit growth of 19% for the first six months. As I said, we have impairment impacts in the quarter.
If you look at it from an EBITDA perspective, then we have an EBITDA growth for the first six months of 32%. Next slide, please. Lars spoke to that we're upgrading our full year sales outlook, and that's why I said H1 is benefiting from growth and net adjustments and an easy comparator. On the contrary, the H2 has a tough comparator because it was facing growth from last year. The 25%, implied in the H2 of this year to get to a midpoint of our guidance range actually requires underlying growth closer to a 30% mark if you take the comparator into account.
Really talking to an acceleration of underlying growth in the H2, driven by our GLP-1 franchise, and of course, enabled by scaling of supply chain. Operating profit, it's important to note that since we issued guidance at Q1, we had the impairment of ocedurenone, which had a 6% negative impact. And then the sales upgrade we did this quarter has a four percentage point positive impact on our operating profit growth.
We really have a significant flow through.2% up on sales growth, 4% on OP. A really solid gearing in terms of financial performance. Of course, I was about to say that translates into a step up in our forecast to free cash flow for the year. That takes us back to you, Lars.
Lars Jørgensen
President and CEO, Novo
Yeah. Just in summary, we are executing well on progressing towards our strategic aspiration for 2025. We're very encouraged by the growth momentum we have. We have scaled our supply chain to be able to continue that trajectory in the H2 of the year, as Karsten just alluded to. We have really exciting pipeline readout also coming in the H2 of the year. Strong start to the year and even more to come. With that, I think we should close on the slides and get to the Q&A. Please take a seat.
Martin Lange
EVP and Head of Development, Novo
Thank you, Lars. Thank you for that presentation. That leaves us with more than half an hour for the Q&A. As per usual, please state your name and your institution, and we'll have one question per person, so we'll take multiple rounds. We have some mics going around, and I think we'll start with James as per tradition, our host.
James Quigley
Executive Director of European Pharma and Biotech Equity Research, Goldman Sachs
Thank you. James Quigley from Goldman Sachs. Just starting on Wegovy net pricing. I think there's a bit of confusion here on the development following the call around some of the comments on channel mix, rebate adjustments, competition, et cetera. Could you take us through how you expect the Wegovy net prices to develop and what are the key impacts from the rebate adjustments that we saw in the quarter?
Lars Jørgensen
President and CEO, Novo
We'll not get into guiding specifically on net price development for individual products, but I'll just say that we don't see any, say, change in the marketplace. What happened in Q2 was that we had a one-time, one-off true-up for rebates given last year. Of course, if you look at the book of business and, say, the sizable rebate adjustments or rebate accruals we make when we end up knowing, understanding, you know, the real flow of products and true-up that, you know, that can lead to, say, changes in the quarter. These are, when you look at the total book of business and the yearly flow of business, down to a very small adjustment for that, say, business.
I think it's difficult to adjust the business based on one quarter when you have these. We have to look at it in totality. With the guidance upgrade we have given, you know, that's value. You can take that as a sign that, I think we have strong value development in our business, and that's what leads to the upgrade we see here.
Jacob Martin
Head of Investor Relations, Novo
Thank you, Lars. We'll move over here to Jo.
[Analyst 1]
Analyst 1
Thank you. A question for Martin, please. In the past, you've said that you don't think that there are any scalable small molecules and that the market will largely remain in the injectable space. Since those comments, we've seen a couple of small molecule GLP type drugs. I wonder if you could update us on your view as to how the market's going to split between injectables and orals. Also, if I can just ask how you're going to choose between your next injectables. Should we expect all of them to come to the market, or should we expect you to just only develop one of them, your best?
Martin Lange
EVP and Head of Development, Novo
First of all, on the small molecules, I have actually said that I think monlunabant, from a scalability perspective, seems to be an attractive offering. Obviously, right now we're working on demonstrating safety and efficacy of monlunabant, but from a scalability perspective, it seems to be, by conventional wisdom, a true small molecule that can be easily scaled. When we look at what else is out there, and of course, we're looking through the same lens as investors. Is it safe and can it be scaled? Most of what we see out there is from a chemistry perspective, slightly more complex than conventional small molecules. That basically means that they are more difficult and more expensive to scale. Of course, if you do the investment, you can scale.
The question comes to what number of patients. The way we think about this and the way that we scale, as you've seen our investments in the subcutaneous space, you would have to invest quite substantially to be able to scale those small molecules to an impactful degree. I think Karsten and Lars can talk more to that. From a pure chemistry perspective, they are not trivial. Of course, they can be produced, but they will not be sort of conventional small molecules that you can just produce to, let's say, two, three million patients, double-digit million patients. Specifically for our own pipeline, we see obesity as a complex disease.
For us, obviously, to have the leading molecules in the incretin space, but also working on new modalities based on amylin biology, based on CB1 biology, that allows us to cater to different patient needs. The way that we look at this, and this is maybe more Camilla that should speak to that, if we see clinical medical differentiation between our molecules, we expect them to be able to coexist to cater to different patient needs. That's the way that we build our pipeline, both in the oral and in the subcutaneous space.
Jacob Martin
Head of Investor Relations, Novo
We move over here to Pete.
Peter Verdult
Managing Director and Pharmaceuticals Analyst, Citi
Thanks, Peter Verdult. Hello. Can we move to actually insulin just for a second and give Wegovy a rest for a bit? Just can you help us understand why there was such a positive rebate adjustment given what we've seen in terms of the insulin price cap and changes there? When you think about IRA next year, is it really gonna matter? Are insulin prices really already at rock bottom, or is there gonna be another downdraft when the IRA hits on some of your insulin portfolio? Thank you.
Jacob Martin
Head of Investor Relations, Novo
Thanks, Pete. Casper, will you give that a go on insulin technicalities and underlying movements?
Karsten Knudsen
EVP and CFO, Novo
Yeah. For insulin, back to Lars' comment from before, when we estimate the gross net in the US, we sell to wholesalers and charge list price, and then it takes, like, three, four months before we receive rebates. The rebates can go to different channels at different rates. That's the estimates going into it. That's also what happens for insulin. We had a bigger adjustment in Q1, but also an adjustment in Q2 based on these estimates. I don't think it benefits anyone in here to go into the gory details about what channels and what rates and what channel mix.
It is true that the insulin growth in the US was very significant in Q2, and it was all driven by price adjustments or rebate adjustments in Q2 of this year. Underlying, when we look at it, insulin in the US is a declining market in terms of market growth. Our market share is also declining, linked, amongst other items, to the Levemir product discontinuation.
Jacob Martin
Head of Investor Relations, Novo
Thank you, Casper. We'll move to Emily.
Emily Field
Director and Head of US Biopharmaceuticals Equity Research, Barclays
Hi. Thanks. Emily Field from Barclays. It seems that there's been, you know, growing concern also coming from the FDA regarding the safety of these compounded formulations of GLP-1s. I was just wondering, you know, with your lowest dose remaining on the drug shortage list and no doses of tirzepatide, at least from what we see on the FDA website, does that mean that compounders can still make your drug and not theirs? You know, how much does the growth of compounding concern you, both from a patient safety perspective and then also taking what share, you know, could be Novo Nordisk?
Jacob Martin
Head of Investor Relations, Novo
Thank you, Emily. I'll give that to you, Lars, on that shortage.
Lars Jørgensen
President and CEO, Novo
Yeah. Just to underline, there's only one sema, and that's produced by Novo Nordisk. I don't know what compounders, well they compound, but I don't know where they get API from and what the quality of that is. We've also seen that I think some of the safety reportings has, you know, there's been a high representation from compounded drugs. We take patient safety very seriously, and so does, you know, the US FDA. Specifically on your point, we have in dialogue with the FDA removed the drug shortage notification on the other doses. We have all along said that we wanna dynamically start patients in a way where they can have a good journey on the titration doses.
We actually scale capacity significantly, so we could in principle have to all decide also to remove, you know, the shortage notification on the starter dose if we wanted to. I just think that we've been out consistently saying to physicians and also FDA that we wanna have a responsible approach to starting patients. You can trust and when you start treatment with Wegovy from Novo Nordisk, we take care of you in the sense that you can titrate up to the doses. That led us to keep the notification on the starter dose, but we could in principle have taken it away also because we still, you know, manage the doses. When we look at it, we have significant step up in capacity.
We allocate that to different doses, and that leads to a significantly higher number of total scripts in the US market, and that's what fuels the growth, and that's what turns into this upgraded outlook. How we look at individual doses and also say classify that from a drug shortage notification. Those are minor tactics, and we could have taken them all away if we wanted to, but we're just saying for consistency because we have said that for some time, that we stick to that. Whether that leads into massive compounding, I don't know, because we could just remove it, and then there was no compounding. I don't think compounding is a way forward generally to serve patients.
Jacob Martin
Head of Investor Relations, Novo
Thank you, Lars. We'll move to Sachin.
Sachin Jain
VP, Bank of America
Sachin Jain, Bank of America. Can I just take one clarification on that last point, and then I'll ask my CB1 question? I think there was confusion on the lower dose yesterday 'cause it was answered two different ways as to whether the 0.25 was gonna grow or not grow. I just interpreted from your answer just there that 0.25 can grow, but it's just not within the boundary of how the FDA defines shortage. I just wanna clarify that before I ask my CB1.
Lars Jørgensen
President and CEO, Novo
Yes. It can grow. Now I'm just thinking, hypothetically, we could allocate all our capacity to produce a starter dose, and we would have new scripts explode. But we wanna make sure that patients can start and titrate to high doses because that's good for the patient, but it's also good for our business because we get, you know, we grow the business by that. Don't put too much emphasis into underlying individual doses because it's totality of the business and how we allocate our capacity to produce that matters. I hope that's clear.
Sachin Jain
VP, Bank of America
Thank you very much. CB1, there's a lot of focus, and predominantly on the CNS safety. I wonder if you could just frame for us how you're thinking about it on two metrics. The GLP-1 psych adverse event rates in the high single digits, I think if that's correct for Wegovy. What delta relative to that would give you comfort or discomfort? And then on suicidal ideation, Acomplia was about 0.5%. In 600 patients across the two studies, we're literally talking about one, two, three events. If you see any, is that a problem? How many patients would you need to see low suicidal ideation before you get really comfortable in the safety profile? Thank you.
Martin Lange
EVP and Head of Development, Novo
The way we think about this is that it's a little bit going back to Jo's question, we aim to scale monlunabant to a great number of patients. That basically means that we need to the level that we can exclude concerns about an excess of neuropsychiatric side effects. To your own point, in any clinical study, there will be patients who report neuropsychiatric events. Just to give you an example, in the SELECT trial, we had 10 events of suicidal ideation on placebo, and we had 10 events of suicidal ideation on semaglutide, so no excess. We intend to take the same approach for monlunabant.
At the end of the day, through the two ongoing phase II studies, a reasonably large, more than 600 patients, additional phase II study continuously de-risking the asset. Obviously our bigger development program to generate with actually a dedicated focus on this specific issue, enough data to say we don't see an excess risk as compared to anything else out there. That's sort of our approach, but that is also the bar. I think that's our bar, but that would also be the bar from regulators.
Jacob Martin
Head of Investor Relations, Novo
Thank you, Martin. Thank you, Sachin. We'll move to the table at the back. Mark Purcell first.
Mark Purcell
Managing Director, Morgan Stanley
Mark Purcell from Morgan Stanley. A question on obesity timelines. A lot of your competitors are trying to accelerate their programs, doing relatively small phase II studies and taking those to the FDA and looking to go into phase III or phase II and parallel phase III studies together. In terms of amycretin, can you help us understand the probability you can go from a couple of phase I studies, one phase II ongoing in diabetes to a full phase III program, both for the oral and the injectable side? Then following up on what Sachin was just asking, I mean, I don't think you learn a lot from an additional 600-patient phase IIb study with INV-202.
If you see 15% weight loss in the obesity study with no excess of grade 1, grade 2 CNS events, what would stop you from moving into phase III straight away?
Martin Lange
EVP and Head of Development, Novo
Maybe I take the last question first. I disagree a little bit in the sense that if you look at the historical data where we have seen neuropsychiatric side effects with other compounds, in one specific example, 30% of patients reported neuropsychiatric events in the development program, 30%. Most of these reported the events quite soon after treatment initiation. That basically means that with a sample size of 600 plus two additional studies that also amount to almost 600 patients, you have a reasonable volume, and you have a reasonable exposure duration to say with any likelihood before you make or I convince Karsten to make Phase III investments, we have excluded the safety events.
Again, there are no guarantees until we have the phase III data, but given the historical data, I think the sample size and the duration of exposure will take us a long way. If we see those three studies, phase II studies come together with no excess safety concerns and let's say 15% weight loss, I'm super happy. Then I will try to convince Karsten to invest in phase III. Could you remind me the other question?
Mark Purcell
Managing Director, Morgan Stanley
On amycretin.
Martin Lange
EVP and Head of Development, Novo
Yes. At the end of the day, you have to have a reasonable assumption and exposure to secure that safety is reasonable to go into phase III. That is why the combination of the phase I studies that we've done in obesity and these type 2 studies that we are currently initiating will be able for us to potentially make a decision during the course of 2025 to say, maybe we can go directly into phase III. If we do that, in the phase I studies, we have to see clear differentiation on efficacy, on safety, and on pharmacokinetics, so we can pick the right dose. It's down to our risk willingness to say, do we want to go into phase III? Have we picked the right dose? Do we believe the efficacy?
Do we believe the safety? We also had to convince the authorities that we have sufficient safety to take that leap of faith. We've in our history done that twice, one with Xultophy and one with CagriSema. I feel confident that we've sort of gotten that process right. It's not easy, it's not trivial, and certain things have to be in place.
Jacob Martin
Head of Investor Relations, Novo
Thank you, Martin. We'll stay at the same table with Richard Vosser. A reminder on one question per person, please.
Richard Vosser
Managing Director, JPMorgan
Thanks, Jacob. Just one question, which would be just you mentioned it at your behest to remove the starter dose cap, and you're managing that. Is that a removal in 2025 or is that a removal in 2026? How should we think about the step up into 2025 and beyond in terms of the overall doses? When are you comfortable enough on supply?
Martin Lange
EVP and Head of Development, Novo
If you look at what has happened the first six months, we have grown total scripts from 100,000 to 200,000. That's a significant number of doses. The debate about what is starter dose, what is titration dose is a bit irrelevant in a way because with the guidance we have and with the comparative Karsten spoke about, if you start doing the math in terms of how many doses are going to the market in the H2, that's significantly more doses. I mentioned before, you know, if there was a priority on starter doses, we could just produce all the starter doses, and we would be flooding the market, and the new scripts would be skyrocketing. That's not a sustainable patient journey.
We wanna, you know, do what creates a good mix, titrating up. That's what fuels the growth and also creates, you know, best efficacy of the product. The whole discussion about starter doses and new scripts is becoming less relevant. It's a total number of scripts across all doses that matters. When you launch a product, it's new script and starter doses. Later on, it's actually, say, the total book of business. It's, in a way, not a, say, a 24, 25 decision because we manage this dynamically to create the best possible growth and patient experience.
Jacob Martin
Head of Investor Relations, Novo
Thank you, Lars. We'll move to Simon, same table.
Simon Baker
Partner and Head of Global Biopharma Research, Redburn Atlantic
Thank you. Simon Baker from Redburn Atlantic. First, a quick clarification on Sachin's question on the CB1 development program. Are there any specific exclusion criteria from the studies related to the suicide ideation risk? Then the question I was gonna ask, going back to what I asked yesterday, on the monthly dose form. You're not there yet. I was just trying to get an idea of how far away you are, what the challenges are, because others are in this space as well. Is this a question purely of formulation? Is it about the specific pharmacokinetics of the molecules you're trying? So how to pin you down on a date, and I'm sure you won't give me one, but how far away is a monthly injectable formulation as a viable product? Thank you.
Martin Lange
EVP and Head of Development, Novo
Specifically for CB1, for us, it's a journey, depending on data. If we get through the first two studies, which are excluding certain patients, without any new psychiatric side effects in excess, then we will discuss what exclusion criteria we will have for the next phase II study. We'll open up a little bit more. If we do that, and that also comes out in a good way, then we can maybe have no or very few exclusion criteria in phase III. It has to depend a little bit on the data. If at the end of the day, we have to have an exclusion in our label, I think that is also acceptable.
Right now, obviously our full aspiration would be that they should be for all, but it has to depend on the data. On the once monthly, there are many technologies that you can apply for sort of extended delivery. Our approach is always first to focus on efficacy and safety. If we can make that more convenient, then we'll do that. We have tested one once monthly asset in clinic. It was honestly not a viable clinical profile. We're sort of going back to the bench. In research, we are still pursuing, as far as I can see, at least three different ways of protecting administration. It's not our biggest priority.
It is a priority because we still see efficacy, safety driving any decision in this space. Obviously it would be good for us to have that offering as well. Therefore we are looking at it. I think for anyone, maybe apart from one player, if you're not in clinic, you are still at least six years away from bringing it into patients.
Jacob Martin
Head of Investor Relations, Novo
Thank you, Martin. We'll move over here.
[Analyst 1]
Analyst 1
I just wanted to briefly touch on the Catalent transaction. It's been going on for some time. How do you today feel about the likelihood of reaching a beneficial, you know, mutually beneficial agreement with first Eli Lilly and then, with all the other potential complainants, all the other parties?
Jacob Martin
Head of Investor Relations, Novo
Karsten, on Catalent transaction?
Karsten Knudsen
EVP and CFO, Novo
Yeah. We're still confident that the transaction will close by the end of the year. We had a lot of advice before entering into the transaction in the first place, in the beginning of this year. We believe that we have a solid case to get to a close of the transaction towards the end of the year. We look very much forward to that.
Jacob Martin
Head of Investor Relations, Novo
Thank you, Karsten. We move to Alexander.
[Analyst 2]
Analyst 2
Thank you. I had a question on China. You have approval for Wegovy in China. You have a very short patent window there, two years to go, I think. Can you just comment on whether you still retain a lot of optimism around the China opportunity? The noise being made by the generics is getting louder all the time. There are plenty of people who are gonna have a pop at this market. Do you have any indication about how quickly you've gone off with Wegovy in China?
Jacob Martin
Head of Investor Relations, Novo
I'll give that to you, Camilla, China on MedNeed and Wegovy.
Camilla Sylvest
EVP and Head of Commercial Strategy and Corporate Affairs, Novo
Yeah, thanks a lot. In China, there are more than 200 million people living with obesity, and we see a great opportunity to make a difference in terms of Wegovy in China. What is important, of course, is that we have a very strong presence in China in terms of our regional presence, in terms of our ability to launch new products. We have worked, you know, in China also in competition with locals before. We at the moment do not see anyone sort of being represented in the short term on Wegovy. We feel as long as we continue to bring innovation to China, we will continue to be a step ahead.
Our understanding from dialogues with Chinese authorities is also that they very much value the innovation that we actually bring to China. Over time, there will be most likely, as we've seen before, a system in China that would allow local generics to produce and to compete. So far this has been constructed in a way where there's always an incentive to bring innovation to China. As we are a very innovation-based company, we are quite happy to see now that all of our new products, Wegovy, Rybelsus, and so on, including also a once-weekly insulin, have approval in China much faster than in the past. This actually allow us to keep to compete even faster in the Chinese market than just five years back.
Jacob Martin
Head of Investor Relations, Novo
Thank you, Camilla. We'll move to Rajesh.
[Analyst 3]
Analyst 3
Hi, good afternoon. Can I just clarify your REDEFINE 1 comments earlier in terms of this. This is not my question, by the way. I want to ask about rebates. On REDEFINE 1, are you going to do a trial control with semaglutide or tirzepatide rather than placebo and compare neuropsychiatric there, or is it just going to be a placebo control and then you'll see other-
Karsten Knudsen
EVP and CFO, Novo
without going into details, there will be an active comparator, there will also be a placebo comparator, there will potentially also be combination therapy in that study.
[Analyst 3]
Analyst 3
Understood. Very clear. Thank you. On rebate, you mentioned that you get data back from the wholesalers two to three months. If my very preliminary understanding of how the accrual accounting and the IT systems work there, you probably are guessing at the moment the level of rebate you have booked in for Wegovy this quarter, right?
Karsten Knudsen
EVP and CFO, Novo
Correct.
[Analyst 3]
Analyst 3
And-
Karsten Knudsen
EVP and CFO, Novo
Just to be precise, we don't get the data from the wholesalers. We get data from the insurance companies. We charge the wholesalers at list price.
[Analyst 3]
Analyst 3
Yeah.
Karsten Knudsen
EVP and CFO, Novo
The rebate claims come from the PBMs who get the claims, of course, through pharmacies and that's where we get them.
[Analyst 3]
Analyst 3
I would imagine that given the projection you've made for your full year, you have assumed that there would be a step-up in volumes, therefore a step-up in rebates in the H2, and therefore you've reflected that in the prices you've assumed for the quarter.
Karsten Knudsen
EVP and CFO, Novo
No. The prices for the quarter, that's an estimate based on the volumes we sold. We make an estimate linked to what channels, and under what formularies, and hence conditions and rebates have they been sold to.
Lars Jørgensen
President and CEO, Novo
The upgrade for the H2 takes into consideration what pricing will be, and that we upgraded value.
[Analyst 3]
Analyst 3
Yes. Thank you.
Jacob Martin
Head of Investor Relations, Novo
Thank you, Karsten. Thank you, Lars. We'll move over here. Before that, just a reminder in terms of one question.
Ben Jackson
Equity Research Associate, Jefferies
Hi. Yeah, Ben Jackson from Jefferies. I was wondering if you have background data on what happens to patients on Wegovy that's discontinuing at around six months, maybe longer. Are they then re-challenging on a GLP-1? And are you seeing switches between GLP-1s there? And do you expect over the longer term that people aren't gonna take this as a one and done and are willing to go back on after discontinuing?
Jacob Martin
Head of Investor Relations, Novo
Camilla, will you give it a go?
Camilla Sylvest
EVP and Head of Commercial Strategy and Corporate Affairs, Novo
Yeah, thanks a lot. We keep in mind that six months is an average stay time, and it's based on experience in the US, where we've seen some interruptions to supply in the past. We continue to be very encouraged about the development of that stay time. When we look at, you say, other countries where we haven't had that interruption of supply, we've seen that, for example, in Denmark, where people started on treatment beginning of 2023, you know, a big part, very big part, close to 90% were on the treatment also at the end of the year. We are continuously, you know, encouraged about stay time.
When we look at different groups of people, we see stay time is significantly longer for people that have been on Saxenda before. Maybe they are more prone to usage of a GLP-1. We also see that stay time is significantly longer with people that are living in, so to say, more affluent areas, so more on the East Coast than the South of the US. You know, also in terms of age, we see stay time being longer for people older than 30 to 40 years compared to younger and so on. Keep in mind, six months is really impacted by all these things.
Having said that, you know, close to, or more than 80% of Wegovy scripts are to patients that are naive to therapy, meaning they have not been on therapy before. Of course, there are some switches between GLP-1s, but I think this is close to, you know, if we look at competition, they are sourcing probably around 10% to 11% from Wegovy and so on. There will always be sort of changes of that, but the majority of all patients starting on obesity treatment are new to treatment. You know, just based on the fact that obesity really hasn't been treated to a large extent before. We are still in the early days of a very low percentage of the total population being treated.
Jacob Martin
Head of Investor Relations, Novo
Yeah. Same table.
Richard Vosser
Managing Director, JPMorgan
Hi there. Another question, if I may, on Catalent. I wanted to ask if you have a sense of how quickly you can ramp up on the fill finish lines? Because my understanding is that most of them are under a contract that might take a while to expire. Thank you.
Jacob Martin
Head of Investor Relations, Novo
Karsten, I'll give that to you.
Karsten Knudsen
EVP and CFO, Novo
Yeah. We do have a good sense of that because that's the core of the entire decision case to access additional capacity. Do bear in mind that we are already working with Catalent as a CMO. There are lines working for Novo Nordisk already with Catalent. What we're getting is additional capacity on the different lines at the different sites. Of course, we honor the contracts that are in place with the existing customers. They have to run off. Let's say the deal closes by end of this year, then we'll have to do technology transfer to the new lines also during 2025.
You could say additional capacity beyond what we have already contracted as a CMO will gradually start from 26 and onwards.
Jacob Martin
Head of Investor Relations, Novo
Thank you, Karsten. We'll go to Emily. Oh, sorry. Yeah, over here, same table.
Kritika Talia
Analyst, Berenberg
Hi, Kritika Talia from Berenberg. Just a question on Wegovy access. We've heard that certain employers have reversed their initial decisions to provide access to obesity medications just because of the escalating demand and associated costs. Is this a trend that you have seen? Related to that, could you just provide us an update as to your current formulary access and specifically the proportion of covered lives that have employer opt-in? Thank you.
Jacob Martin
Head of Investor Relations, Novo
In terms of the employer opt-ins, Camilla, would you give that a go?
Camilla Sylvest
EVP and Head of Commercial Strategy and Corporate Affairs, Novo
First of all, we have, you know, more than 50 million patients being covered in the US, so very strong access. Around 80% of them pay up to only $25 per script in terms of self-pay. When it comes to opt-ins, there will always be opt-ins and opt-outs, but we continue to have a net opt-in, so to say, of employers. It just means that we continue to broaden our access.
Jacob Martin
Head of Investor Relations, Novo
Thank you, Camilla. The last question will go to Emily before we round off.
Emily Field
Director and Head of US Biopharmaceuticals Equity Research, Barclays
Hi. Emily Field from Barclays. A somewhat similar question, but going back to the question of stay time, you know, how much do you think that insurance coverage in the US deflates or dampens stay time just with people switching jobs, aging into Medicare, and so they might not have coverage to that degree? I mean, do you see that as also a big dampening effect in addition to supply constraints?
Camilla Sylvest
EVP and Head of Commercial Strategy and Corporate Affairs, Novo
Yeah. I think, you know, there will always be people that may opt from one team to another where they are not covered or so, and that of course happens. Given that 50 million lives are covered, I think we don't need to be preoccupied with the potential in terms of coverage. Also keeping in mind on stay time, it's really in the first sort of 60 days that we really see the drop-offs, probably part of getting used to GLP-1. Then once people continue to stay on, they stay on longer. Keep in mind that if six months is truly an average, and you have to think about the variation in this.
Of course, that's also why there's significantly higher stay time for people who have been on GLP-1 before, most likely because they are either used to, you know, you know, being initiated on GLP-1, knowing more what to expect, and therefore, the average stay time is much longer. Think about it much more like that. We think, you know, we're treating one million patients now, but 50 million being covered, this is not what is, you know, what is holding anyone back. To the point from before, we're truly scaling production, you know, to be able to supply more doses into starter doses so that people can start and continue on the treatment. That's really what we are working on right now.
Jacob Martin
Head of Investor Relations, Novo
Thank you, Camilla. Before handing it over to you, Lars, for final remarks, thanks to everybody in the room for coming and for everyone online for dialing in. In case of any follow-ups, please reach out to Investor Relations. Lars, final remarks.
Lars Jørgensen
President and CEO, Novo
Thank you. I hope it comes across that we are very pleased about where we are as a company, both in terms of our traction with, say, sema and other products, not least in the US market. We upgrade because we have more supply coming, and we upgrade in value, so don't need to worry about, you know, the price per script, so to say. A lot of questions. I appreciate that on pipeline because we have a really exciting H2 of the year, not only in growth point of view, but also in terms of inflection points for pipeline, and I think Martin had some good points there. Thank you very much for your interest.
We look forward to share more details on all these aspects, as they evolve over time. Thank you.

content.text:
Daniel Muusmann Bohsen
Head of Investor Relations, Novo Nordisk A/S
Good afternoon, everyone. Welcome to the revamped Sterling Square at Citibank. Good afternoon to everyone in the room and to those listening in on the webcast. Good morning, good afternoon, good evening. It's been a very busy week for earnings and other events. We are ending the week on a high with the Q1 London Roadshow of Novo Nordisk. The speakers don't really need introduction, but just notice Karsten, Group CFO, Camila, Group Commercial Strategy Head, and last but not least, Martin, Head of R&D, joined by an array of investor relations. Now, usually I'd be saying without further ado, hand straight over to Karsten for some slides and some Q&A.
[Company Representative] (Citi)
Company Representative, Citi
I think it is worth us just pausing and recognizing that it is Daniel Muusmann Bohsen, his last function as the head of Novo investor relations. I think that needs to be sort of recognized by the audience in the room. Not just yet, not just yet. Got a few more words to say. On that note, I have known Danny, I think, for over 15 years. He was a Willis Towers Watson, Novo junior IR, and I was still a Willis Towers Watson analyst covering Novo Nordisk, and we were discussing Insulin and Victoza back in the days. I think with Martin's blessing, he was sent off to Colombia to go and sell some drugs. Then came back in 2020 to be a head of investor relations.
I think we can all agree, being head of IR in 2020 to 2024 for Novo, not a bad place to be. Daniel, I mean this, and hopefully I'm speaking on behalf of everyone here and on the line, you know, your professionalism, your patience dealing with people like ourselves, your responsiveness, helpfulness, and just all around being a good bloke, really appreciated. We wish you well on your next venture with Novo Nordisk. Plenty of good times I'll have to say. Just call out, I think New Orleans 2016 was a particular highlight. Thank you for making that one special. Just before we say goodbye, Daniel, and wish him well, I do have a little gift for you.
It's within my compliance policy of less than $25. It is to help you immerse yourself in the Taiwanese culture. Daniel, on behalf of everyone here, I do wanna say thanks for everything and good luck going forward. Thank you. I will be asking Karsten about Taiwan and the sort of change in performance over the next few quarters under new management. Thank you.
Karsten Munk Knudsen
EVP and CFO, Novo Nordisk A/S
Great. Thank you, Pete, for those nice words to Daniel. We are all sad he's leaving, but we're also very much looking forward to follow him in Taiwan. You know, we have a materiality assessment on what we report externally in terms of our segment split and so on. Every week we'll be tracking in our weekly sales if Taiwan sales is becoming big enough to include in the quarterly external announcement. We're all rooting for you, Daniel, for Taiwan to make one of the coming quarters. Thank you to Pete and Citi for hosting in your beautiful new premises here. Nicely revamped, so we appreciate that.
then we're bringing another strong quarter from Team Novo in terms of performance. continued growth, continued momentum from last year, amongst the strongest growth stories in the industry, as you know, and we keep pushing that. as you know, the future's uncertain, and it might play out differently. hence we have a nice deck with a forward-looking statement included, so no further details on that. every quarter, we bring a status on our strategy execution, and I'm not gonna go through all the details. you'll hear a lot more about it in the coming hour. just to say on the environmental side, we keep pushing forward.
Now we started reporting on full Scope one, two, and three. You see that being up 32%. There's one singular key driver for our CO2 emissions being up that much. That is the fact that we're building a lot of new factories, which goes directly into our scope three emissions. We don't take it lightly, but now we're fully transparent around our environmental footprint. 42 million people now on Novo products, up 4 million compared to a year ago. Continued strong commercial execution that Camila will come back to. I think actually one of the biggest years ever in Novo history in terms of the magnitude and importance of R&D readout.
I'm getting an echo from the new audio. I'll keep talking. The net 24% sales growth. Really pushing on all fronts. You'll hear much more. Without further ado, over to Camila on commercial execution.
Camila Sylvest
EVP of Commercial Strategy and Corporate Affairs, Novo Nordisk A/S
Thank you, Karsten. Just to recap on our sales growth numbers, this Q1, we had 24% sales growth, 30% operating profit growth. EVP and CFO, Novo Nordisk A/S
Yeah. Since it's probably me being quoted, I better stand up for it. This is completely as expected. Right. What we're looking at in the market is that this is a volume opportunity, and we're very happy with the market access we have in the U.S.. We have more than 50 million people with obesity covered in the U.S. today. Our market access is very good. Of course, we work with the payers to ensure that we have the appropriate market access that ensures this level of coverage or even more. Of course, the market is also defined through competition and a competitive entry.
There are no surprises in pricing in the U.S.. Just reminding you, this is a significant volume opportunity. The 50 million people with obesity that we have covered for today, we are only serving a fraction of that, less than 1 million.
Daniel Muusmann Bohsen
Head of Investor Relations, Novo Nordisk A/S
Thank you, Karsten. That concludes the Q&A session. Before giving the word to Karsten for his final remarks, I just want to say thanks, Pete, for the kind words, and thanks to all of you that many of you I have met many times over the last four years, and I've truly enjoyed the conversations, the challenging questions, also the pushback. Thank you so much and please remember to keep them on their toes also in the future. Karsten, over to you. Any final words?
Karsten Munk Knudsen
EVP and CFO, Novo Nordisk A/S
Very briefly, thank you for joining again. You feel we're on a roll. Amazing levels of sales growth continuing into this year, 24%, for the quarter, turning into attractive profit growth, 30%, for the quarter at the current exchange rate. Our innovation machine is really also on a roll in terms of readouts and what you just have seen thus far between SELECT, FLOW, and hopefully, to be replicated into the near future, on the coming readouts. Very strong push on innovation for the rest of the year. Thank you for your attention and we'll be around for another quarter or so. Looking forward to discussing more detail. Thank you.
