content.text:
Richard Vosser
Equity Analyst, J.P. Morgan
Right. Welcome everyone to Novo's Q1 roadshow. I'm Richard Vosser at J.P. Morgan. It's a great pleasure to have the Novo management team here for this roadshow. Karsten, CFO, Camilla Sylvest, Head of Corporate Strategy. Exactly. Martin Lange. Martin is Head of Development. I'll hand over to Karsten for a few introductory remarks in the presentation. Thanks, Karsten.
Karsten Munk Knudsen
EVP and CFO, Novo Nordisk
Great. Thank you, Richard, and thank you to J.P. Morgan for hosting this launch presentation. Thanks to all of you participating in person. It's always good to interact in person. I'd like to remind you that this launch session is being recorded, so just for general use. We have a great team here in London, and we released our results last week. You could say it's not as fresh as we had anticipated. The reason why we released our numbers, as I'm sure you're aware, basically, you know, we have to follow the Danish regulations for listed companies in Denmark.
When you have identified material information, then you have to go really fast without any undue delay and report as fast as possible. That entails a lot of hard work from you know everybody in the organization and the board meeting, et cetera. It's not something we take lightly. The benefit for you is that then you had the weekend also to prepare for this launch session. The session for today is, I'll say, reasonably snappy on the presentation.
Then we have a good time for Q&A and perhaps also a bit of time afterwards in a breakout if you didn't manage to ask your question at the launch session. I have to remind you about forward-looking statements, and we just saw this again, that predicting about the future can be hard and real events might fall out differently. That's how the world operates. In terms of our strategic aspirations as a company, we launched a concept back in 2019, and we updated a couple of them at our latest Capital Markets Day. This is how we report to the market on an ongoing basis.
Just to cover some of the key components in terms of our purpose and sustainability, our ESG performance, we continue to drive performance both on CO2, which is, of course, not getting easier this year because people have started to travel and product distribution is moving a notch more towards air distribution, linked to the kind of our supply chain situation. Still down compared to 2019, but not as much down as last year.
On our social responsibility piece, I think it's a great achievement by Martin and the development team that now we have a positive scientific opinion around our thermostable insulin solution that basically enables our human insulin to be stored at below 30 degrees Celsius for a month, which is really a key feature in developing markets. Really something that can make a difference. The reason for the European registration is that then we can reference that in all these countries where it would be more relevant, where perhaps there's less access to electricity and so on. Finally, diversity and inclusion, also a key priority for the company to continue to progress on that.
On our pipeline, which Martin will come back to later, after last year where it was more of an investment year and trial execution year. Now we're starting to see some really good trial readouts. You saw some at the Capital Markets Day between Mim8 and CagriSema. Now you've seen ONWARDS 2, the first phase III results, favorable phase III results with the once-weekly insulin. We're really happy about that, as you will hear later on. Of course, the high-dose Ozempic in the US marketplace. Commercial, we keep performing against our aspirations or even ahead of those aspirations. Some of you will remember our initial obesity aspiration about doubling obesity. That's actually exactly what we did in Q1 compared to Q1 last year.
Really fantastic traction on our obesity franchise these days. All of it turning into a great sales growth of 18%. Actually the strongest sales growth in relative terms in 2 decades of Novo Nordisk and the biggest absolute sales growth quarter-over-quarter ever in the history of Novo Nordisk. Really amazing performance in terms of commercial execution and turning it into financial results also at 18% operating profit growth. I'll come back to that in more details. In terms of capital allocation, we had very strong cash conversion in Q1 and also allocation to shareholders at DKK 20 billion.
A lot of value allocated to shareholders in terms of both dividends and share buybacks.
With that, I'll hand it over to Camilla to cover our commercial status on commercial execution.
Camilla Sylvest
Head of Corporate Strategy, Novo Nordisk
Yeah. Thanks a lot, Karsten. Good morning, good afternoon, everyone, I should say here in London. You know our sales growth, 18% sales growth driven by a combination of a strong growth in international operations of 13% and North America operations growing 24%. We also see nice growth in each of the regions here, EMEA, China, and Rest of World. So all units contributing to growth. When we look at therapy area distribution, you see, the 18% is clearly driven by a growth in GLP-1, where we see continued growth in North America of 38% in our GLP-1 franchise, of 60% in international operations.
We see on insulin a growth rate of -4%, driven by a -15% in the US, but a slight increase of 1% in international operations. As Karsten was alluding to, 7% growth in our obesity franchise, driven by a 146% increase in North America operations and 63% in IO. We have a continued single-digit growth in our rare disease franchise. If we zoom in on two of the biggest growth areas, if we start with GLP-1, especially our Ozempic franchise, you see here the 4 weeks rolling estimates of how prescriptions have really picked up in the beginning of this year on an NPRX level.
On the right-hand side, you see the TRX level, a very steady performance increasing the Ozempic share of the total GLP-1 segment. The short-term increase is driven by additional focus from our side on DTC, but of course also on more doctors prescribing Ozempic. We see better pick up now in lower tier segments also, and of course, there might potentially also be a halo effect to the semaglutide molecule in general. When we then look at the Wegovy here, you see the uptake on the total scripts, so TRX, and of course, we have not been promoting Wegovy the last quarter in the US. Despite that, we now still see a continued uptake, but we have also 80% coverage now in the commercial segment.
We are currently not promoting the three lowest doses. We don't want patients to be initiated if they cannot continue on the treatment. We have now seen that our contract manufacturer is initiating the commercial production, so we expect to be back in the market with supply in the H2 of this year and making our product available again. That's the plan for Wegovy in the US and how we expect this to continue. With that, I'll just hand it over to Martin to talk a little bit more about R&D.
Martin Holst Lange
Head of Development, Novo Nordisk
Yeah. Thanks very much, Camilla. As Karsten already alluded to, this is gonna be an exciting year in the R&D space. We'll have a lot of interesting readouts, obviously starting with the icodec, but certainly also potentially we'll SELECT later on in the year if we get to do an interim analysis. We see very nice progress across all our programs. We have, as you know, phase III programs ongoing in all of our therapy areas, which is an interesting place to be, especially when we see those reading out in the years to come. Just wanna call out two things in the diabetes space. First of all, obviously, as you know, we've got the 2.0 milligrams semaglutide approved in the US for the treatment of Type 2 diabetes.
That is very, very exciting, also because you've seen the data, you've seen the results based on the publication. Now we have it into the label, very nicely describing the benefits of 2.0mg versus 1.0mg, namely more glycemic control, more weight loss, but no difference in the safety tolerability profile between the two doses of semaglutide, and also a very nice description of the cardiovascular benefits of semaglutide, not sort of distinguishing between 1 and 2mg. So a broad label calling out good efficacy, good cardiovascular safety, and good safety and tolerability. Doug and his team are launching as we speak. We talked about the ONWARDS 2 program. This is truly exciting. From our perspective, I think you've seen the program, the ONWARDS program. It's six trials.
It spans Type 1, it spans Type 2 diabetes. It's a global program. It even has one study, ONWARDS 5, that caters to payers, potential payer discussions. It's a real world evidence study with the potential of demonstrating A1C superiority, exactly what payers are looking for. That would be a first, I think, in insulin treatment, having real world evidence available at time of launch to cater to that discussion, and obviously we're a bit excited about that. ONWARDS 2 was the first study to read out. We're still waiting for the next five studies to read out. It was, in some aspects, the most difficult and therefore also the most interesting study that we had to look at because the comparator was insulin Tresiba or insulin degludec.
Degludec, as you know, really efficacious drug, but also probably the most hypo-safe insulin, basal insulin that we have out there. Going up against Tresiba in our first readout was obviously interesting. Patients were your garden variety Type 2 diabetes patients, A1C at baseline between 7 and 10, all patients being treated with basal insulin at time of randomization. Any basal insulin. Approximately 30% of patients came from Tresiba, the rest came from various others, other basal insulins, primarily insulin glargine. Patients were randomized to either insulin icodec or insulin degludec. Really interesting. Obviously you've seen the headline results, which were truly exciting. This is a treat-to-target study. That's the regulatory requirement from the FDA perspective. That means that for 100 years, what we've seen when it comes to insulin development is non-inferiority on primary endpoint.
You guys have commented and asked about that in recent years. Why don't you see superiority if you think this is a better insulin? Basically because we had to do this treat-to-target. Probably also to an extent because there was maybe not that much to differentiate on other than the risk of hypoglycemia. Now we have a once weekly insulin with a super flat and stable profile. Just remind you, insulin icodec has a peak to trough over a week of 14% difference, so really stable. To be compared with 80% in, for example, Glargine and Levemir, and 40% for Tresiba. Really a flat and stable profile. That actually pans out even in a treat-to-target setting into superiority on A1C. That's a first.
In 100 years, we've never seen that in this kind of study. That is in and of itself quite encouraging, obviously making us quite optimistic of what comes next in the next five studies. What is really also important is no difference in hypoglycemia. I've heard some of you talk about there's a numerical difference in hypoglycemia, which is obviously true. You've seen the numbers. It was 0.25 and point 73. Just to remind you again that in previous studies with basal insulins, hypo rates have been in the vicinity of 1.4 to 4 events per patient per year. Here we're talking about less than 1 in both treatment arms. Basically means that a patient on insulin icodec has to wait 1.5 years before he or she gets a non-severe event of hypoglycemia.
When we talk about non-severe, we saw no severe events of hypoglycemia on insulin icodec. We actually did see severe hypoglycemia with Tresiba in this trial, and therefore again, speaking to the safety of this compound. Another first is actually a significant improvement in quality of life. Significant not only from a statistical perspective, but also from a clinical perspective, again, speaking to the benefits of this molecule. Camilla asked me, will we get the triad of efficacy, safety, and convenience? I think the answer is yes. There's even another upside with insulin icodec, and that's on the environment. Going from 7 to 1 injection per week. That obviously also have an impact on how much plastic, how much glass do we have to put into landfills. I think in 2022, that's not a trivial thing to have added as an added benefit.
Not in the bag yet, still waiting for the last five trials, but a very, very strong start for Icodec.
Karsten Munk Knudsen
EVP and CFO, Novo Nordisk
Thank you, Martin. I'm head of development, really happy with the insulin icodec. We'll get back much more on that in the quarters to come with the five additional trials. Looking at financials, you've all been through this as part of our release, but just recapping 18% sales growth at constant exchange rates taken into reported 24% sales growth, given the tailwind from especially the US dollar. Really significant sales growth on a big base. Gross margin adjusted for currencies reasonably flat.
Of course, one thing worth noting is when you look at our employee count, as we also have in our company release, which is up 9% over the last year, the biggest single driver of that is actually increase in manning in manufacturing. As we talked about, scaling manufacturing, part of that is also scaling employees to, you know, all the classic of, you know, seven shifts, three shifts, seven days a week. In terms of sales and distribution cost 18%, it's a classic. It's investments in Type 1 diabetes as well as obesity market development. No news there.
R&D up 29%, being of course impacted by our Dicerna acquisition and the run rate of Dicerna, which is actually also what you see in terms of the step up in other operating income, compared to our Q1 last year. Net-net Dicerna in the Q1 has a negative impact on our P&L to the tune of 2%. Adjust for that as potentially some companies would do, then actually our operating profit growth would have been 20%, excluding Dicerna. Apart from that, our R&D costs are really being driven by our focus to expand our pipeline and diversify, and a lot of investments going into both research and development.
From a therapeutic point of view, investing significantly in what we call other serious chronic diseases, so our cardiovascular franchise, as well as NASH, and trials in that area, Alzheimer's. All in all, 18% operating profit, 28% reported in reported terms. We have the hedging going the other way. That's how it is when you hedge the US dollar for 12 months. A very good hedging efficacy here in the beginning of the year and the net profit growth of 13%. That start compared with the NBRx trajectory you saw with Camilla led us to step up our outlook and raise our outlook significantly, I would say from before 6 to 10 and now 10 to 14.
You see how it drills down throughout all our financial ratios. Pretty much no surprises there from top line all the way through to cash generation, and increase share buyback to now DKK 24 billion. That covers kind of the warm-up commentary, and now we move into Q&A. I think we're a small audience, so let's do one, maximum two questions at a time, and then I'm sure we can ping back, ping around, back and forth. I'll just sit down, and then I'll give it to Richard to have the opening question as our host.
Richard Vosser
Equity Analyst, J.P. Morgan
Thanks, Karsten. Maybe two then. Firstly on Camilla, you mentioned commercial access 80%. I think before the opt-in was sort of 40%. Could you give us an update on the opt-in level from commercial employers into that? And then secondly on Ozempic 2 milligrams, you've highlighted, I think Doug highlighted on the conference call, that it will be priced in line with other doses for diabetes. How do you manage that given the brand is very close in the dosing to Wegovy? Does that have any impact on Wegovy in terms of cannibalization or yeah.
Karsten Munk Knudsen
EVP and CFO, Novo Nordisk
Thanks, Richard. There's two for you, Camilla, one on opt-ins and the other one for pricing of 2.0.
Camilla Sylvest
Head of Corporate Strategy, Novo Nordisk
Yeah. Yeah, Richard, we are approximately in a situation where we have 80% coverage, gross, and then we have about half of the employers that opt in, so that means a 40% net coverage, so slightly more than what you recall from before. It continues to improve, but it's a long list of employers that we're of course working with. It does consistently improve. On delivery on messaging, it's very, very important for us of course to stay completely true to what is the label, and we promote Ozempic in diabetes care, and right now we don't promote Wegovy in obesity care, but we will hopefully get back to that.
For us, it's extremely important to stay completely in line with that, for good reasons, for business ethics reasons. Nevertheless, we do see a pickup in the scripts of Ozempic, as I just talked about, also because we're expanding our prescriber base. Of course also because Ozempic is recognized for its triad of benefits, HbA1c lowering, strong weight loss, but also the significant cardiovascular risk reduction. All of that, you know, with the increasing awareness of course builds more and more momentum for Ozempic.
Karsten Munk Knudsen
EVP and CFO, Novo Nordisk
Thanks, Camilla. Just a bonus info on the coverage for obesity, as you would have seen, now we have a contract with Department of Defense also. In addition to continuing to enroll more employers on the commercial, of course we're also working with some of the public employers in terms of getting access, whether it's under certain Medicaid plans or Department of Defense. I think we have good progress, so very happy with that. I think we move to Wimal.
Wimal Kapadia
SVP and Head of Investor Relations, Novo Nordisk
Great. Thank you very much. Can I just come back to Richard's question, actually? So Ozempic high dose is priced at the same level as Ozempic 1 milligram. But that's only 0.4 milligrams less than Wegovy. If the net price of Wegovy is similar to Saxenda, that's a 30% premium on Ozempic net price. I'm just curious, how do the payer discussions go? Because for 0.4 milligrams, that incremental dollar price is quite a lot. I'm just curious how you know, do you have a different rebate for the 2 milligram than the 1 milligram? That's the first question, just following up on Richard. Then the second one, again, probably for Camilla. The GLP-1s are clearly doing really well.
If we think about the diabetes market long term, so if the bookends are metformin and insulin, and they're relatively stable at about 14% metformin, 20% insulin roughly, so it's coming down, but slowly. You have 40% of diabetes volumes to play for. What is the peak penetration for GLP-1s in the US? You know, is it 25? Is it 30? How much do we need to leave for the SGLT2s long term? Then I guess tied to that, what does that mean for the rest of the world? You know, can Europe and the rest of the world get to that US level? Thanks.
Karsten Munk Knudsen
EVP and CFO, Novo Nordisk
Thanks, Wimal. I counted two and a half questions on that one. So, thanks for pushing the limits. I think we'll let it pass this time around, then we'll get back at you another time. So, Ozempic 2.0 pricing, I'll give that a shot, and then Camilla, if you can talk to GLP-1 volume slash patient penetration, US slash rest of world. So yes, on Ozempic 2.0, it's diabetes pricing. That's what we see also from competition. I think the way you should look at it is it's a flat pricing between 0.5, 1, and 2.
From a payer point of view, you buy the portfolio, and actually a lot of patients are still only at the 0.5. It's a flat price across, but the blended volume, so to say, per patient is—let's see how it all plays out, but will be perhaps, you know, less than 1mg, depending on the time horizon. You have that, and then you have different price point in obesity. That's one key point to consider.
The other key point is of course that having, you know, formularies in two different disease categories, so to say. Of course, the formularies in terms of managing the formularies and the opt-ins or whatever step edits or whatever to get access to the medicines are different and hence caters for differentiation from a payer point of view also in terms of how they manage their categories in terms of could even be co-insurance designs could be different between those categories. We spoke about the opt-in also from on Richard's point of view. The categories are being managed different by the payers also vis-à-vis their customers. Camilla, on GLP-1 penetration.
Camilla Sylvest
Head of Corporate Strategy, Novo Nordisk
Yes. GLP-1 penetration, very dependent on the launches of new products and the efficacy that we see. We now are in Europe and in the US on a volume basis, sort of 8% to 12% of the market, but we do see that it is significantly picking up. Of course, a lot of this is related to the continued benefits that we see, the cardiovascular risk protection, weight loss and HbA1c loss. Just to give you an example, from China, where we've seen now reimbursement of Ozempic, then we have seen the market size of GLP-1 out of the total grow from 1% to now being closer to 7% or 8%, and that in a very short time frame.
Basically, of course, if you look at the volume growth, you see that this segment is growing approximately 30% in volume, roughly, you know, across most regions of Europe and US. You would see other segments of the market growing a lot less. I think if you apply that dynamics, assuming that whenever there are new launches into the segment, then of course it keeps fueling the market growth rather than cannibalizing itself, then I guess you can try to understand how to do the math of what this could be. It's clear that the benefits of GLP-1 are very, very strong when we just compare HbA1c and weight, and also cardiovascular risk profile versus some of the other compounds in the market.
I think that's the best way to look at it, to try to understand what could this become? There is also in guidelines now an increased focus on treating with GLP-1s right after metformin. That's another support to this class.
Karsten Munk Knudsen
EVP and CFO, Novo Nordisk
Great. Thanks, Camilla. Move to Pete, Peter Verdult. That's the guy with the nice tie, Mark.
Peter Verdult
Research Analyst, Citi
Thanks, Pete Verdult, Citi. Two questions. Sorry to harp on about this, but I'm gonna expand on the questions from Rich and from Wimal. You know, in a couple of years, you're gonna have a quite formidable competitor turning up where that whole GLP-1 pricing offset between obesity and diabetes is gonna be gone. That's obviously how should you or we be thinking about how you navigate that? Because all the responses you've made so far are all fair, but that dynamic is gonna change quite considerably in two years. I'd like you to just discuss that. Secondly, I asked this this morning at the breakfast meeting. I mean, most of the industry have talked about, you know, responsible price increases, no more than inflation. Obviously now inflation is 7% to 8%.
Is Novo going to eat it, or do you think you've got the ability to, you know, put up your list price increases to protect yourself from inflation? Thank you.
Karsten Munk Knudsen
EVP and CFO, Novo Nordisk
Yeah, Camilla, if you cover the first one vis-à-vis, I think we explained clearly, you know, where we are today. What could be the scenarios vis-à-vis Lilly and what approach could they be pursuing and how would we think about the market dynamics on GLP-1 pricing? Then I'll cover inflation and how we try to mitigate that.
Camilla Sylvest
Head of Corporate Strategy, Novo Nordisk
Yeah. What we see now increasingly is that obesity is being reimbursed for Saxenda outside of the US in an increasing number of markets. Of course, when reimbursement happens, then prices are of course not the same as before reimbursement and out-of-pocket. Of course, in the same to Karsten's point from before about the different channels in the US, by the time that you would expand into other channels, it could be Medicare, for example, over time, if we get the Treat and Reduce Obesity Act in place, then of course, it's likely that prices will converge towards each other. I think that's the dynamic that we are working towards to make sure that more and more patients can get access to obesity treatment.
You know the numbers that just a very few percentages are being treated despite a huge unmet need. I think that's what we are pursuing and I think that's what I should comment on and actually not what Lilly is more likely to do. You should check with them on that. I do think that over time prices are likely to converge. Of course, this is offset by the volumes and there is a very big demand as we have noticed, of course, also in the recent year.
Karsten Munk Knudsen
EVP and CFO, Novo Nordisk
Yeah. Thanks, Camilla. Of course, let's see what Lilly does. That's completely on their prerogative. I think they've been out commenting, you know, different scenarios also in terms of how they could go to market. We'll have to wait and see. On inflation and how to mitigate inflation. The classic premise of inflation, we all see it and the numbers, whether it's 7% or 8% in the US, etc. Running a company, the starting point for mitigating inflation is one, pass on the increased cost to your customers, that you see across many industries. Secondly, how do you fend off inflationary pressures from your suppliers?
If I take the last one first, then in terms of suppliers, then of course we get the pressures from our suppliers. We have a rather mature procurement setup, so in terms of being clear about the contractual settings we have in our contracts with our suppliers. You know, some of these contracts, you know, just doesn't open for, you know, for suppliers to increase prices. Some there's a lag effect, and some they can break the contracts or whatever. So I think we have a very mature setup there to minimize the immediate inflationary pressures. But clearly it is something that will happen.
On the cost side, we mitigate that through efficiencies and resource allocation, and then we're in the fortunate setting that as a rapidly growing business we also have some margin leverage to work with. We actually do have a number of levers to alleviate fully or partially the inflationary pressures we face as a company. Reminding you just, and I don't think I have to remind you, but mathematically of course we are in a better setting than low margin industries. Being a high margin industry of course, just in relative terms, it hits us at 40+% operating margin less than other players, other industries.
On the sales side, I think it's fair to say that in a number of markets, it's hard to kind of reopen contracts, especially in some like European markets that we have negotiated a price point for our products, and hence it will be a very cumbersome lengthy process if at all possible to open up. In some emerging markets, countries or IO markets, especially in hyperinflationary markets, there already exist mechanisms for basically changing our prices. That could be markets like Argentina and Turkey. Actually, if you go to the appendix of our company announcement, you can see how we adjust for hyperinflation in terms of our reporting in order not to overstate our constant exchange rate growth.
We are actually backing out some of the hyperinflationary price increases in these markets. We do have mechanisms in place. In the US, we are negotiating, you know, contracts for next year as we speak, not concluded. That's one out of many elements going into these negotiations between, you know, formulary positioning, competitive pressures, et cetera. Of course, inflation is one of the arguments there as are many other aspects. I think that's as clear as I can be on that one.
[Analyst 1]
Analyst 1
Sorry, just on the same topic. You talked of the volumes earlier. The volumes are very strong. Given the inflationary environment, does that slow down any pricing pressure that you might see? Can you use that as an argument? You've obviously got the volumes to your advantage. Yeah.
Karsten Munk Knudsen
EVP and CFO, Novo Nordisk
Yeah, you would say the best way to fend off price decreases if you're in a US setting is that you are differentiated enough and you have the highest possible market share because then of course the harder it gets for payers and PBMs to throw you off formulary. Clearly, on one hand side, when we show strong demand for our products like the Ozempic trajectory on volume and share, then of course the payers would be very cautious to remove from formulary because they will have a lot of their customers that will be unhappy if they cannot get the product that they wish for.
That's on one hand side. Of course, on the other hand side, when you are effectively a procurement organization and you see value pockets increasing rapidly, then of course you have to consider how to deal with that cost increase. That's kind of the balancing factors and that's of course their PBM job. As we've said all along, our strategy is to grow the volumes and to maintain choice for patients, so ensure basically co-preferred formularies in the T2D market in the US.
[Analyst 1]
Analyst 1
Sorry, just on that. I should know that, I'm sure you've said, but the upgrade to the sales guidance, the growth, is that all volume? How much of that is volume? And it's all volume, right, versus price?
Karsten Munk Knudsen
EVP and CFO, Novo Nordisk
I'd say for all material purposes the upgrade in guidance is driven by increased Ozempic volumes. Mark?
[Analyst 2]
Analyst 2
Thank you, Karsten. Two R&D questions. I know I sound very busy today. First one, I think most KOLs believe that the SELECT trial is gonna be successful. It's described as being a sort of pivotal trial for the future of obesity medicines, so really important you get this right. We're all sort of focused on Q3 in this potential interim. We've had CVOT studies reading out early before, and it sort of damages their potential when it comes to discussing with payers and governments and guideline policy makers and things like that. I'm thinking number needed to treat as opposed to percentages here, particularly when it comes to CV death and all-cause mortality.
I guess, you know, if we say roughly 26 months into the trial, you know, 4.5% event rate to that point, 17% benefit, that's not a massive number needed to treat, if you stop early. Can you help us understand what the stopping criteria are that ensures that you do not lose the power of this potential study? I mean, you know, a lot of KOLs are thinking you should do a primary prevention study and just wait and see what happens. It's really important you get this one right. That's the first question. The second one is really quite simple.
Icodec in the real world, if we see severe hypos, which I think most people feel there will be some, how do you treat a severe hypo with Icodec relative to obviously a normal insulin, given that you're gonna have, as you said, I mean, insulin levels will be pretty stable at, you know, to the tune of 14% over a week. Presumably you have to stay in hospital, you have to stay under some medical care for longer. I'm just interested in that point of view.
Karsten Munk Knudsen
EVP and CFO, Novo Nordisk
Thanks, Mark. That's two for you, Martin. SELECT stopping rules and the pros and cons of doing an interim vis-à-vis the stakeholders. Secondly, on Icodec, how do we treat severe hypos in a real-world setting?
Martin Holst Lange
Head of Development, Novo Nordisk
Yeah. Actually, I like that you call it a simple question. The answer is gonna be a little bit nerdy and a little bit complex. I think it's a super good question. It's obviously something that we've been looking at, and in all practical purposes, when you do an RCT for 26 or 52 weeks or however long you do it, that's real world because you send the patient home. They are basically stuck with that potential problem. We haven't seen it. We have exposed, at this point in time, 5,000 patients in the ONWARDS program. We've not seen this issue. We look obviously at prolonged hypoglycemia. We haven't seen it.
We also look at what some call repeat hypoglycemia, so that would be several events of hypoglycemia within a day, where the patient may be able to eat basically their way out of hypoglycemia, but then when the food is gone, they go back again. We haven't seen it. I mean, the flat and stable profile in and of itself protects a little bit from that. But the other thing is, and that's the nerdy part, and I apologize to my colleagues for that one.
Karsten Munk Knudsen
EVP and CFO, Novo Nordisk
Not to the audience.
Martin Holst Lange
Head of Development, Novo Nordisk
Not to the rest of you. You had to hear it, and you have to learn it. Camilla already knows it, so she can also say it.
Camilla Sylvest
Head of Corporate Strategy, Novo Nordisk
I knew it.
Martin Holst Lange
Head of Development, Novo Nordisk
The way that icodec protection works is that it binds to albumin. That basically means that level of albumin, all others being equal, the albumin and the insulin receptor compete for icodec. As you also know, if the insulin receptor is being occupied by insulin, it's being internalized into the cell, so therefore it cannot bind anymore. That basically means that if you have not sufficient insulin receptors, icodec will simply be stuck on the albumin. That actually in and of itself creates, at least in theory, a very nice buffer to prevent hypoglycemia. The other thing I actually
I probably shouldn't, but I take a little bit comfort in is that in the ONWARDS 2 program, since it was a switch study, we had to load the patients with icodec to secure that they got up to a sufficient plasma concentration. That basically meant that they had to start the first treatment, the first week, with 150% of expected insulin dose rather than 100%. We had eight patients who inadvertently stayed on 150%, for longer than one week. That basically means that they were in fact overdosed, and they did not experience severe hypoglycemia.
I think even though that was obviously a mistake, and we need to really optimize in the marketplace our communication around how to do that switch, it actually speaks to the safety and the robustness of the icodec molecule that, I mean, even in that space, you don't introduce severe hypoglycemia. I mean, I should never say never, but what we've seen so far, it looks really good, and it looks really safe. That was a long question to a simple answer. On the other one, I'm not really prepared to go into numbers and details, but you all know that we sample sized the main part of the SELECT trial for 17% differential on efficacy on MACE on the primary endpoint.
If we do an interim analysis, our instructions to the DMC, that's the independent body that looks at the data, is that whatever sort of happens while closing down the trial has to be a sufficient differential to secure that the approximately 100 events that will be accrued while we close down the trial cannot change the dynamics and the conclusion of the trial. That basically also mean that if you do an interim, the differential that will be in excess of 17%. Not in a trivial amount, it will be sort of in excess of 17%. I don't want to give the number, but that also means that that would be highly statistically significant. It will obviously be clinically relevant.
I think Camilla, if we just see on the good side of 17%, she will be happy from a commercial perspective. That also means that for some of the secondary endpoints that are also of clinical relevance and probably also of both regulatory and payer interest, they would with some likelihood also be statistically significant or at the very least be going in the right direction.
Karsten Munk Knudsen
EVP and CFO, Novo Nordisk
Right. Thank you, Martin. Let me move down the line to Theo.
[Analyst 3]
Analyst 3
Hi. Quite a lot of questions. I will keep it to two and then come back if possible. Camilla, given what we know of ONWARDS 2, and Martin noted your point, it's not yet in the bag, you've still got five studies to come. But-
What would be a good or a bad outcome relative to market shares of the basal insulin market for icodec in 3, 4, 5 years' time? Secondly, you kind of gave us a long list of reasons why Ozempic's been really strong, and I think all of those make perfectly logical sense. But the one you did not mention was potential use of Ozempic while there is Wegovy supply constrained. So I'm wondering if that is, are you saying that's not what you are believing, and consequently when Wegovy does come back to the market in H2, you're not expecting to see any sequential decline in Ozempic US volume over Q1? Or should we be assuming that you will have some flow-through into Wegovy, and therefore there'll be sequential decline on Ozempic?
Karsten Munk Knudsen
EVP and CFO, Novo Nordisk
Thanks, Kayo, for those two questions. I'm actually looking forward to hear the answers on both. What Icodec market share will make us satisfied, Camilla, in the basal segment, and if you can predict Ozempic indirect levels for the next couple of years-
Camilla Sylvest
Head of Corporate Strategy, Novo Nordisk
Yes.
Karsten Munk Knudsen
EVP and CFO, Novo Nordisk
I would also be really happy on that one.
Camilla Sylvest
Head of Corporate Strategy, Novo Nordisk
Thanks a lot, Kayo. You just turned this into my budget meeting. I really appreciate it. Those questions. I have a guy here next to me taking notes, and we follow up forever on the answers. Market share on icodec, we talked about earlier, we have 37% share in value and 33% in volume in the basal segment. Of course, this is significantly lower than what we've seen in other segments, the premix segment, for example, or even the fast-acting segment. Having a superior offering on HbA1c that gives you no more hypos, but equivalent on hypos a very, very low weight, if you really have to wait for a long time to see any hypos based on what Martin explained, and also a quality of life that is significantly better.
This is of course very, very important, and taking all of that together has a potential to, of course, transform the way we look at basal insulin. I would hope that we can make a significant inroad into the basal segment. Probably we should just see the rest of the ONWARDS trials before we get closer to what could a good aspiration level be. I do think that we need to be able to make something really good out of this for the sake of the many people that are truly concerned about hypos, but are also struggling with trying to understand how they should, you know, remember their doses on an everyday basis. We know more of them forget to take their daily insulin injections.
I also personally look forward to the more real life, the results of the trial, where we leave patients more alone, for a year's time to see, what that looks like. Because of course, compliance with a once weekly is likely to be higher, everything else equal. I know I don't give you the market share answer, but at least what potential-
[Analyst 3]
Analyst 3
Majority market share on the basal insulin?
Camilla Sylvest
Head of Corporate Strategy, Novo Nordisk
Sorry?
[Analyst 3]
Analyst 3
Majority market share in the
Camilla Sylvest
Head of Corporate Strategy, Novo Nordisk
Majority market share is, we can always discuss whether we discuss the absolute or relative, but that we can come back to. I think that's enough for now until we've seen the rest of the ONWARDS trials. Appreciate the support from the room here on, maybe to Martin, I hope.
Karsten Munk Knudsen
EVP and CFO, Novo Nordisk
I'm taking notes.
Camilla Sylvest
Head of Corporate Strategy, Novo Nordisk
Yeah. On Ozempic, actually, we did discuss, you know, we have seen more prescribers from lower tier segments prescribing, and we also understand the relevance of GLP-1, the very strong Ozempic's performance in terms of approximately 80% getting in good control, we know from our clinical trials. So a really great number of benefits. That of course drives our continuous performance with Ozempic. I also spoke a little bit to the halo effect. There's probably an increased understanding of what this molecule can do, semaglutide. And of course, we cannot rule out that some people are living with diabetes thinking if I can, and they that they heard about what this product can do in terms of weight loss, and then they're interested in that.
I don't have any evidence to suggest that it's all, you know, off-label use or that it is, but I think it's very, very important for us to promote Ozempic for diabetes care and Wegovy for obesity care. I think I would leave it with that part. Would we then later on see a decline in Ozempic? That's of course part of what one has to consider. Would there be, whenever we are fully supported on Wegovy, some people who have, even living with diabetes, that have easier access to Wegovy this way than Ozempic? That's still to be seen, but these scenarios of course we try to cater for in the guidance that we have given you.
Karsten Munk Knudsen
EVP and CFO, Novo Nordisk
Yeah, just adding to this one, you know, forecasting indirect is pretty much really complicated, and it's even more complicated to forecast the conversion from NBRX to TRX, just to make it even worse. What we saw last year was kind of interesting. When you looked at NBRX and then mid last year, there was also, you remember, the step-up in the NBRX linked to potential halo effects, et cetera. We saw a step-up, and then we saw the curve continuing from the step-up. I'm not saying we'll see the same now, but it's, you don't find these very simple direct correlations, at least based on historical data. I think it's Sachin, and then we move the other way.
[Analyst 4]
Analyst 4
Thank you. I might just take a follow-up on icodec hypos to Martin's question. I remember from the summit receiver, there was a lot of debate around various hypo definitions. My question is fairly straightforward. In an answer to the question, you talk about no severe, no repeat, no prolong, but you clearly had an excess of clinically relevant, whatever it was, less than 3 millimoles. Just to understand why that happened as to you've got three metrics that you're trending favorably on and then one that you're not. What's the driver there? The second question is if you could spend a little bit more time on ONWARDS 5 as to what conversations you've had with payers.
Now that you know a lot more about the molecule from the first study, what are your expectations in a real-life setting for what level of A1C, and can you get hypo superiority? If that's all you get, and then sort of one very quick one on semaglutide. Having seen tirzepatide, would you consider a semaglutide, tirzepatide head-to-head in obesity?
Martin Holst Lange
Head of Development, Novo Nordisk
Thanks, Sachin. Three questions. You beat Wimal. One, Martin, I think you called hypo nerdiness. Yes, kind of indirect effect question. Then ONWARDS 5, why did you design that based on the payer dialogue? Then semaglutide versus tirzepatide. Yes. We'll start from the beginning. On the hypoglycemia, again, I think it's important to call out when we see a numerical difference at a very low level. I don't wanna belittle the difference, but it's sort of comparing one to two and then say you have a doubling in risk. This is also why there's no statistically significant difference. It's basically a function of really few events.
Another way of looking at this is you may have seen the number of, or the proportion of patients reaching an A1C below 7. If you do that proportion, I think it's around 40-something versus 20-something. The interesting thing is if you then make the analysis reaching A1C below 7 without hypoglycemia, it's the same numbers more or less. Again, speaking to the very low rate of hypoglycemia. Absolutely a difference. But at a level where it's difficult to say, is this clinically relevant? I don't think it is. You'll also see when we don't compare to tirzepatide, I mean, next study reading out will be ONWARDS 1 versus glargine. We know that there is a different hypo risk associated with that comparison.
I think you'll see some maybe slightly different results. If we can repeat what we've seen so far, I think both not only we but also our future customers will say this is a safe molecule. ONWARDS 5, we basically I think at the very least, Camilla and I probably also Karsten have shared a frustration that we from a regulatory perspective were forced to do treat-to-target, and that means going for A1C parity. From a payer perspective, they don't really care. We saw that with tirzepatide. We came with what we think was very nice hypoglycemia data, and payers said, "Well, we can't pay for that.
We would like to see A1C difference." We wanted to change that outlook for icodec, so we had a dialogue with some US payers, some European authorities, the Chinese authorities. We asked them, "What are you looking for?" Very clearly, you had to demonstrate A1C superiority. We know now also based on ONWARDS 2, that is a potential, also in ONWARDS 5. They very clearly stated, we want to see real world data. The problem in doing treat-to-target is that in our RCTs, we can get more than 50% of the patients to a certain target, and in real life, that doesn't hold true. Therefore, they wanted to see what happens with real life. We've never been able to do that.
With the advent of digital tools, monitoring, collecting data on remote advising on insulin titration through an app and an algorithm, that basically allowing us to virtually give the patient the app on an iPhone, the insulin and monitoring device for glycemic control, and then saying, "Goodbye, we will see you in a year." Obviously, we do have some visits, but I think it's four visit in a year.
[Analyst 4]
Analyst 4
Just what have the payers said to you in terms of the relevant 1 A1C difference?
Martin Holst Lange
Head of Development, Novo Nordisk
They haven't. Historically, we have been looking somewhere between 0.2 and 0.4, depending on who you are talking to. I think again, in a 26-week study versus tirzepatide to see statistically significant 0.22, that's a very nice place to start because it could give us the aspiration of going maybe beyond that in ONWARDS 1 and 5. Final question was CagriSema head to head with tirzepatide. Sitting next to Camilla, I feel very confident that if the data that we see so far with CagriSema holds true all the way through phase III, I don't think I would mind doing a head to head because as you've also heard me say before, I do think that CagriSema will hold its own on efficacy.
We have very high aspirations for that. On the safety and tolerability side, so far we've seen something that is not additive, but actually just the sum of what is semaglutide. That means that CagriSema holds the potential for being competitive on both efficacy and safety. Obviously, I would like to see the data before I commit, but if it holds true, then we are all in. Great. Thank you, Martin. Thank you, Sachin. We have time for two more questions, so I'll say it's two persons and one shot each. Joe, you are the first one.
Jo Walton
Research Analyst, Credit Suisse
Okay. Can I ask a more thought experiment? If sales growth continues closer to the level that you've seen in Q1 than you expect it to go back to, because all sorts of, you know, fantastic things happen, the halo effect and all the rest of it. At what level of sales growth do you think we should actually see margin leverage come through? Because at the moment you have the luxury of stronger sales, and you've got lots of ideas, and you can easily reinvest, and everybody still is very happy with that. There must be some point at which there's a diminishing return. You know, you haven't got all the ideas that you need to spend that much money in R&D. Camilla has brought all of the DTC-
Karsten Munk Knudsen
EVP and CFO, Novo Nordisk
I might just have to interrupt here. Of course, we will have lots of ideas in R&D on how to spend money.
Jo Walton
Research Analyst, Credit Suisse
Well, the huge amounts of money that you get if you continue to have sort of 15% top-line growth for any extended period of time. Can you just help us think about that level and where we should think about leverage coming through versus that reinvestment? I am going to sneak in just a very quick second one. Just wondering whether you've highlighted in the past that stay time is significantly less on obesity than it is on diabetes. Have you seen any evidence of people not staying on Ozempic, which would speak to perhaps some of them being there in obesity, or are we seeing much longer stay times in obesity?
Karsten Munk Knudsen
EVP and CFO, Novo Nordisk
Thanks, Jo. Two relevant questions. As you know, also from our strategic aspirations, then we have clearly communicated, even though it's not necessarily translating into all spreadsheets in London and other good cities, that we're working with a stable margin outlook in the medium term for the company. Our clear base plan is also, at higher growth rates, really to be investing mainly in R&D. Right now, you should also bear in mind that, you know, as we spoke about the inflationary pressures, we also have to have some work to do there. We believe we can do it, but that's also a reality.
Clearly, I don't wanna invest in R&D unless I believe it has an attractive return, but that would be the key premise. I think we've shown our financial discipline over and over again. You shouldn't be modeling with upside on operating margin. You should be working on us investing in the long term. This time, we don't have any data, Camilla?
Camilla Sylvest
Head of Corporate Strategy, Novo Nordisk
Yes, that's right. We don't have any evidence of any changes in the stay time.
Karsten Munk Knudsen
EVP and CFO, Novo Nordisk
Right. It's too early, so it'll be half a year, a year down the road. Pete, last set of questions?
Peter Verdult
Research Analyst, Citi
Yes. I promise they're two very quick ones. Just coming back to the Wegovy-Ozempic debate for a minute, just in terms of high dose, can you just remind us, is it generally true that the higher dose GLP-1 to 2 mg is more commonly needed for larger obese Type 2 diabetics, I guess I'm thinking? Is there any correlation between dose of GLP-1 needed versus. Equally, what proportion of obese Wegovy patients from your initial data did have Type 2 diabetes, if you have separate data on that, if you can give us that. Then can I just ask a quick one just on the Wegovy production. You say you want to make sure you've got enough stocks before you open the gates, if you like, given what's happened.
Can you give us some sort of idea what sort of TRX or what sort of patient? 'Cause we have no idea of the rate of production from Catalent, but what are you assuming in terms of that before you do? Can you give us any idea of what you're assuming in terms of the demand before you do then say, "This is enough inventory, we're opening up," to at least give us some sort of idea of the timeframe we're thinking about?
Karsten Munk Knudsen
EVP and CFO, Novo Nordisk
Yeah. If I just take the inventory build first, and the way we do it in terms of sizing inventories, Pete, is we work with a number of scenarios because it is clearly super volatile, what we're looking into, based on our historic experiences. We base the sizing of inventories as a combination of different scenarios, and then we furthermore combine it with our launch tactics, which you should expect to be probably more gradual than a big bang out of the gates. It's impossible to give you one point estimate without for sure be completely wrong.
You have the historic trends both on TRX, gradual uptake, as well as NBRX. It's also how many new starts should we expect and it may take a little bit longer. You know, the big question is, of course, to what extent do physicians have patient inventory, so to say, patients waiting for the product. That's a big uncertainty, and that's what we're careful how to manage. In reality, it's not only a TRX measure, it's also a patient stocking type assessment that we're making. We just want to make sure that it turns into a more controlled approach this time around.
Martin on Sema 2.4 patient profiles and in terms of need of dosage.
Martin Holst Lange
Head of Development, Novo Nordisk
If we start with the dose part, I think you've seen a differential in terms of the dose requirements for glycemic control versus weight. You reach a plateau for glycemic control, for example, on semaglutide. When you reach those 2.0mg approximately that we just gotten approved, you can't get much out on glycemic control moving beyond 2.0mg. On body weight loss, we haven't seen the plateau yet, and that also means that, I mean, first of all, you see a difference between 1.0 and 1.2 in terms of body weight loss. You also see moving beyond 2.0, for example, towards 2.4mg, a further body weight loss.
This is a little bit in opposition to maybe what also we saw last week, where there was actually a plateauing looking at the tirzepatide data that appeared to have sort of reached something between 10 and 15 milligram in terms of body weight lowering. We haven't seen that for semaglutide, like, well, semaglutide yet. We actually haven't established the full ED90 for the weight loss part of semaglutide. On the clinical side, all patients that we've investigated with semaglutide 2.4 milligram have been non-diabetics. I think in the real world, I don't know if we have data yet on patients on Wegovy being how many also have diabetes. I haven't seen the data, but
Karsten Munk Knudsen
EVP and CFO, Novo Nordisk
No, I don't think so.
Martin Holst Lange
Head of Development, Novo Nordisk
So far, I mean, the vast majority of what we have on Wegovy and 2.4 milligrams semaglutide is non-diabetics.
Karsten Munk Knudsen
EVP and CFO, Novo Nordisk
Right. Thank you, Martin. Thanks for joining this Novo Nordisk called Q1 launch meeting. Thanks to Richard and J.P. Morgan for hosting it. I would just like by closing out with the comments that we'll be at ADA, and we'll be hosting a sell-side event at ADA in the US, in early June. I hope to see you all. We will probably do both some type of a sell-side nice sell-side dinner, and then we'll have an investor event with Martin and a couple of his colleagues from R&D. We hope to see you there, hopefully with more data also out of R&D. Who knows?
Martin Holst Lange
Head of Development, Novo Nordisk
We'll do our best.
Karsten Munk Knudsen
EVP and CFO, Novo Nordisk
Thank you, and have a great rest of the day.
Martin Holst Lange
Head of Development, Novo Nordisk
Is it good?
Jo Walton
Research Analyst, Credit Suisse
Yes, okay.

content.text:
Operator
Hello, and welcome to the Q4 2021 Novo Nordisk A/S Earnings Conference Call. Throughout the call, all participants will be in a listen-only mode, and afterwards, there will be a question and answer session. Today, I'm pleased to present Lars Fruergaard Jørgensen. Please go ahead with your meeting.
Lars Fruergaard Jørgensen
President and CEO, Novo Nordisk
Thank you very much. Welcome to this Novo Nordisk Earnings Call for the full year of 2021 and outlook for 2022. I'm Lars Fruergaard Jørgensen, the CEO of Novo Nordisk. With me today, I have Executive Vice President and Head of Commercial Strategy and Corporate Affairs, Camilla Sylvest; Executive Vice President and Head of Product Supply, Henrik Wulff; Executive Vice President and Head of North America Operations, Doug Langa; Executive Vice President and Head of Development, Martin Holst Lange; and finally, Chief Financial Officer, Karsten Munk Knudsen. All presenters will be available for the Q&A session. Today's earnings release and the slides for this call are made available on our website, novonordisk.com. Please note this call is being webcasted live, and a recording will be made available on Novo Nordisk's website. The call is scheduled to last one hour. Please turn to the next slide.
The presentation is structured as outlined on slide two. Please note that all sales and operating profit statements will be at constant exchange rates unless otherwise specified. The Q&A session will begin in about 25 minutes. Please turn to slide three. As always, I need to advise you that this conference call will contain forward-looking statements. Such forward-looking statements are subject to risk and uncertainty that could cause actual results to differ materially from expectations. For further information on the risk factors, please see the company announcement for the full year of 2021 and the slides prepared for this presentation. Please turn to the next slide. In 2021, Novo Nordisk delivered double-digit sales growth and progressed on all four dimensions of our strategic aspirations. I would like to highlight a few today.
Within purpose and sustainability, we continue to take action on our social responsibility strategy, Defeat Diabetes, with a focus on access and prevention. In 2021, we reached almost 35 million people living with diabetes with our treatments. More than 5 million of these received treatment through our access and affordability programs. From an environmental impact perspective, we have also progressed. In 2021, our CO2 emissions across operations and transportation decreased by 43% compared to 2019. Finally, to underline our commitment to offer an inclusive and diverse working environment, we launched a global gender diversity aspiration. The purpose of this is to achieve a balanced gender representation across all managerial levels by the end of 2025. Martin will come back to the specific key milestones within R&D, but I would like to briefly share my overall perspectives.
By the end of 2021, we had ongoing phase III clinical trials within all our therapy areas. 2022 will be an exciting year with multiple interesting readouts from our R&D pipeline. Following a productive partnership since 2019, we acquired Boston-based Dicerna Pharmaceuticals and their innovative RNA interference platform in 2021. Dicerna's RNA interference technology platform is complementary with Novo Nordisk's existing technology platforms. The acquisition supports our strategy of using a broad range of technology platforms across all our therapy areas. We expect to start clinical development with the first target in 2022. In 2021, we delivered double-digit sales growth, reflecting solid commercial execution across geographies as well as across diabetes, obesity, and biopharm. Regarding the supply situation for Wegovy, Henrik will provide an update later. The commercial progress across all therapy areas will be covered by Camilla and Doug.
Lastly, leaving financial to Karsten, we are pleased with the sales growth of 14% and operating profit growth of 13% in 2021, both measured at constant exchange rates. With that, I give over the word to Camilla for an update on commercial execution.
Camilla Sylvest
EVP and Head of Commercial Strategy and Corporate Affairs, Novo Nordisk
Thank you, Lars, and please turn to slide five. In 2021, our total sales increased by 14%. This sales increase was driven by both operating units, with international operations growing 14% and North America operations also growing by 14%. GLP-1 sales increased 32%, driven by North America growing 25% and international operations growing 52%. Insulin sales increased by 1%, driven by 6% growth in international operations, partially offset by a 9% sales decline in North America operations. The US insulin sales declined by 9%, driven by lower realized prices and a decline in volume. Obesity care sales grew 55% overall. In international operations, Saxenda sales grew 52%, and in North America operations, obesity care sales grew 57%. In the US, obesity care sales grew 58%, driven by both Saxenda and Wegovy.
Biopharma sales increased by 4%, driven by North America Operations growing 6% and International Operations growing by 3%. Please turn to slide six. In line with our strategic aspirations of reaching 1/3 of the diabetes value market by 2025, our sales growth within Diabetes Care of 13% is faster than the overall diabetes market. Thereby, we have improved our market share by 0.8 percentage points to now 30.1%. The increase in GLP-1 growth of 32% and market share gains in both operating units.
